Inflation, as explained in the FAQ card, refers to the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth less than it was tomorrow, typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. Causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and while inflation can rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production and supply chain problems contribute to inflation. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. NATO formally invites Finland and Sweden to join the alliance on Wednesday after Turkey lifted its veto on membership, the Secretary General said Tuesday evening, clearing the way for one significant alliance expansion in decades. This historic deal follows a memorandum between the two countries underscoring the war in Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin's efforts to weaken NATO, pushing Sweden and Finland, which have been neutral for decades, to pursue NATO membership. After weeks of talks capped by a meeting in Madrid, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey agreed to lift the block on Sweden's membership in return for actions promised regarding terrorism and terrorist organizations. NATO allies Finland and Sweden commit to fully supporting Turkey against threats to national security, the Secretary General said, providing details of the agreement that includes domestic legislation to crack down on activities entering the agreement, as well as Turkey's extradition requests concerning individuals Erdogan wants sent to Turkey to face trial on terrorism charges. Sweden has already passed tougher legislation on terrorism that goes into effect in July. Finland and Sweden, feeling vulnerable since Russia invaded Ukraine in February and attacked neighboring countries, decided to apply to join the alliance, despite Sweden's long tradition of neutrality. President Putin warned the countries against joining NATO, but the two countries believe their membership will bring benefits to the alliance. Finland shares a 1,340-mile border with Russia and is equipped with a modern army, while Sweden controls the entrance to the Baltic Sea, which will greatly assist NATO in defending vulnerable countries in Eastern Europe. The final push to resolve the dispute started early Tuesday morning when President Biden called Erdogan to urge him to allow discussions on the topics to proceed. According to a senior administration official, who requested anonymity to discuss private deliberations, the substance of the conversation involved Erdogan and the leaders of Finland and Sweden for several hours. Later that night, the two leaders consulted Biden, announcing the agreement. An American official said the deal involved Turkey welcoming Finland and Sweden's applications and addressing issues related to an arms embargo imposed by Turkey. American officials indicated that the days leading up to the agreement played a role in the negotiations, stating that broker countries insisted Turkey, Finland, and Sweden resolve their differences. The agreement was announced Tuesday night, and a senior administration official conceded that diplomatic efforts to publicly minimize U.S. involvement complicated discussions. The next steps for Finland and Sweden are clear, as NATO is set to vote on Wednesday to accept their applications, and a quick study of defense needs is expected. Talks are routine since the countries are NATO partners, but the last step requires current member legislatures to vote on accepting new members, which has historically taken a year. It is expected that much of the process will move quickly, as the Senate is already pressing ahead with hearings on the applications, and Biden is a firm proponent of adding new members.

A Democrat from Connecticut became the first woman elected governor with the right to fill the term. During World War II, many Asian men and women were elected to public office, and the first Asian Americans were elected in California and Hawaii, often winning elected office. The typical process includes submitting a visa application online, paying an application fee at a designated bank, signing up for an interview, and gathering documents to show a stable life, which likely includes recommended documents such as a letter of introduction from an employer, an invitation letter, a passport, bank statements, and anything else that proves the intent to return home. Cases may also be referred for deeper review, where information is checked against American foreign databases, and officers from various agencies may conduct interviews and background research. Everything is checked before a visa is issued, and upon arrival at the airport, American customs officers conduct an additional round of behind-the-scenes screening and may question travelers; applications can be denied, with the highest refusal rates for the fiscal year being for Somalia, Cuba, Syria, Afghanistan, and El Salvador. Members of the visa waiver program in Europe include Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, as well as travelers from Asia, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Singapore, South Korea, and Taiwan. South American travelers from countries in the visa waiver program can visit the United States for up to 90 days without a visa, which is a shorter process that requires a smaller fee; travelers can apply for travel authorization by submitting personal information, including employment, diseases, and criminal history. Inflation is a key issue, affecting purchasing power over time, meaning the dollar is worth less today than it was yesterday, typically expressed as an annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. Causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise or fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation can be detrimental, depending on circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poorer households spend a larger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also impact the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Fed leadership has sharply reduced unemployment while maintaining control over inflation, coming close to achieving its congressional mandate. Special Counsel Robert Mueller III made public remarks Wednesday regarding the Russia investigation, providing a full transcript of his statement. "Good morning, everyone. Thank you. Two years ago, the acting Attorney General asked me to serve as Special Counsel, creating a special office through an appointment order that directed the office to investigate Russian interference in the presidential election, which included investigating links and coordination between the Russian government and individuals associated with the Trump campaign. I have now spoken publicly about the investigation, and I am speaking today as the investigation is complete. The Attorney General has made the report of the investigation largely public, formally closing the special office and allowing me to resign from the Department of Justice to return to private life. I will make remarks about the results of our work, but beyond my remarks, it is important that the written work speaks for itself. Let me begin. The appointment order begins with the interference in the presidential election, alleging that a grand jury indicted Russian intelligence officers, part of the Russian military, who launched a concerted attack on our political system. The indictment describes how they used sophisticated cyber techniques to hack into computers and networks, using private information from the Clinton campaign, and that this information was released through fake online identities and the organization WikiLeaks, with releases timed to interfere with the election and damage a presidential candidate. The grand jury alleged a separate indictment against a private Russian entity engaged in a social media operation where Russian citizens posed as Americans in order to influence the election. The indictments contain allegations of guilt or innocence for specific defendants, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The indictments and activities described in the report illustrate the efforts to interfere with our political system, which needed to be investigated. It was understood among the reasons the Department of Justice established this office that there was also a reason to investigate efforts to obstruct the investigation. The matters investigated are of critical importance to obtain full and accurate information from every person questioned in the subject of the investigation. The investigation lies at the core of our effort to find the truth and hold those accountable. Let me say a word about the report. The report has two parts addressing two main issues we were asked to investigate. The first volume of the report details numerous efforts by Russia to influence the election, and this volume includes a discussion of the Trump campaign's response to that activity, concluding that there was insufficient evidence to charge a broader conspiracy. The second volume of the report describes the results and analysis of obstruction of justice involving the President. The order appointing the Special Counsel authorized us to investigate actions that may have obstructed the investigation. We conducted the investigation and kept the office and the acting Attorney General informed of our progress. The work set forth in the report gives us confidence that the President clearly committed a crime, but we did not make a determination on whether the President committed a crime. The introduction of the volume of the report explains our decision and explains a longstanding Department policy that a President cannot be charged with a federal crime while in office because it is unconstitutional to even charge him, keeping such a charge sealed and hidden from public view is prohibited by the special office's part of Department of Justice regulations, which are bound by Department policy regarding charging a President with a crime. Therefore, the option to consider the written opinion explaining this policy makes several important points. It informed our handling of the obstruction investigation. The points in the report describe two key opinions: the first opinion explicitly permits the investigation of a sitting President, which is important to preserve evidence while memories are fresh and documents are available, among other things, as evidence used to charge someone. The second opinion states that the Constitution requires a process in the criminal justice system to formally accuse a sitting President of wrongdoing. Beyond Department policy, the principles of fairness guided our principles, and we concluded we could not reach a determination one way or the other on whether the President committed a crime. My final position is to comment on the conclusions of the President conducting an independent criminal investigation and reporting the results to the Attorney General, who is required by Department regulations to conclude whether it is appropriate to provide a report to Congress and the American people. At one point, certain portions of the report were requested to be released, but the Attorney General preferred to make the entire report public. I appreciate that the Attorney General made the report largely public. There is certainly a question about the Attorney General's good faith decision, and I now hope and expect that, when the time comes, I will speak in a manner regarding this decision. I was told whether to testify or speak about the matter of discussion regarding my appearance before Congress. The testimony will provide information beyond what is already public. Today, I also want to thank the attorneys, FBI agents, analysts, and professional staff who helped conduct this investigation in a fair and independent manner. These individuals spent nearly two years in the special office with the highest integrity, and the central allegations of the indictments regarding multiple systematic efforts to interfere with the election deserve attention from every American. Thank you."

Inflation FAQ card: inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth less than it was tomorrow. It is typically expressed as an annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. Causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Inflation, defined as the loss of purchasing power over time, means that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow; it is typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, while inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a larger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Unemployment remains in double digits, with millions of new people continuing to file for state jobless insurance each week, and the path forward for government relief remains uncertain as Congress debates extending federal aid for many economic victims, including the extra $600 per week in unemployment benefits that expires in July. Emergency lending programs continue to prove useful, as the mere announcement of these programs has helped smooth markets, although many have been lightly used; officials have warned that conditions could worsen if a second wave of the virus strikes, creating renewed turmoil that may necessitate the purchase of corporate bonds to support the market and asset-backed securities to facilitate lending to smaller businesses.

Track COVID area to get the latest state and county data on cases, deaths, hospitalizations, tests, vaccinations, and the coronavirus, including the latest map, case count, and data sources from state and local health agencies. Cases, deaths, and the Department of Health and Human Services report test positivity, hospitalizations, and ICU patients, along with the seven-day average and average of recent seven days of data figures for COVID patients in hospitals. The recent number of patients hospitalized with COVID in the intensive care unit may see spikes due to inconsistent reporting from hospitals, with hospitalization numbers early in the pandemic affected by incomplete reporting. The federal government reports test positivity based on viral tests conducted by laboratories, while state health departments report to the federal government. States like Washington and Puerto Rico have hospitalizations and test positivity reported based on assigned dates from the Department of Health and Human Services, which is subject to historical revisions. Cases and deaths data are assigned dates based on figures publicly reported, with case and death seven-day averages calculated over days within the range of data reported. The period is extended to include older days, with at least seven days of data included, and the data from days following non-reporting days averaged. Non-reporting days are represented in rolling averages, with days representing multiple days' worth of data always included together. This means instances of timed reporting for the seven-day average and average of seven days may have certain days' total case and death reports excluded, with the average portion of cases and deaths data removed from the average calculation. The national case and death count averages are the average sum of the average number of cases and deaths across states and territories, with the day average matching the average calculated from the case and death total to account for timed case and death reports at the state level.

Inflation is a frequently asked question; inflation refers to the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow, typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services, including food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise or fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market; rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Things change with the new rule; now, when a company buys a stake of less than a percent in another company, it usually accounts for the investment on the balance sheet at the cost price paid at the time. Under the old rules, the value of the investment goes up, but the new rules require that the value be written on the income statement and balance sheet. Behind bars for murder in Maine, individuals can still vote if convicted in Mississippi, but they are permanently barred from the ballot box. According to the new study, roughly a billion people around the world, or percent of the global population, fall into this category, as estimated in a report published today by global health officials, which excluded healthy older individuals without underlying health conditions, a group also known as at risk by age. In late March and early April, the Fed began promising to get the market to buy bonds and actually intervened by purchasing exchange-traded funds that track a broad index of bonds that trade like stocks. By mid-June, the Fed began directly buying bonds that had already been issued, using an index created to guide purchases amid accusations that the central bank was favoring big companies. The Fed officials say they are just trying to encourage smooth market functioning without giving individual firms a boost, helping big employers while implementing policies to safeguard the overall economy. The Fed is taking this approach to buy bonds in order to defend against accusations surrounding its rationale and the lingering controversies around its approach since it first announced in March that it would buy corporate bonds in the secondary market, including one for already issued debt in the primary market.

Climate change discussions take center stage in Glasgow, where we are likely to hear a lot about climate searching for hidden meanings in the context of net zero, sustainability, nature-based solutions, adaptation, and carbon footprints. Electric natural gas governments are committing to net zero, and sustainable products are being sold on Instagram. As banks push for climate action, it seems like everyone wants to know what these terms really mean, as effective communication of information has a long history of choosing words meant to advance agendas. Two decades ago, Frank famously advised Republicans to say "climate change" instead of "global warming," as the latter sounded less alarming, trying to stave off calls for urgent action. A lot has changed since then, as the power of words shapes the way people think about climate risks. Government and business leaders gather in Glasgow while the New York Times climate team compiles a list of terms likely to be heard, along with their context and caveats, such as carbon pricing, carbon tax, renewable versus clean energy, and natural gas versus gas. This guide to the climate debate reveals that while science is clear, the language surrounding it is anything but. Net zero commitments from countries and companies promise to make sure we read the fine print, as scientists warn that global warming will continue to worsen unless humanity reaches a point where we no longer pump additional greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. In recent years, a growing number of countries and businesses have made pledges for net zero by various dates, including the United States and China, with promises from companies like Amazon and Apple. While the theory of net zero sounds like a good idea, in practice, the concept can be easily abused, as governments and companies pledge net zero while often only promising to reduce fossil fuel emissions rather than completely eliminating carbon dioxide. This often means offsetting emissions through methods like planting trees or using technology to pull carbon dioxide from the air, although the effectiveness of these methods is contentious. Critics worry that leaders and businesses use uncertain promises to avoid making deeper cuts today. Many net zero pledges are vague and not backed by concrete policies to curb emissions, particularly in the United States and China, where many corporate net zero pledges lack rigorous targets. The promises usually require plenty of scrutiny, as sustainability claims become harder to believe in a world where a quick online search reveals a vast selection of products branded as sustainable. In many cases, it is even unclear what a company is claiming without independent verification, and the term "sustainability" can backfire. For instance, cotton bags marketed as sustainable may not significantly reduce consumption of consumer goods. In the airline, restaurant, and banking industries, companies often market themselves as sustainable while having little backing for such claims. The United Nations states that sustainability needs to be present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs. True sustainability means bringing humans into balance with the planet's resources, which requires transformative changes and hard work to achieve. The concept of carbon footprint is useful for industries to assess their impact, as it helps individuals understand the emissions associated with various activities, from dining out to heating homes and even pet food. Researchers developed the idea of carbon footprint as a legitimate sustainability research tool, although critics argue that the fossil fuel industry has used it to shift responsibility away from wider structural changes needed to rein in emissions, including a much faster shift toward clean renewable energy. Despite these criticisms, the carbon footprint remains a useful concept, allowing us to see that the carbon footprint of a typical American is many times that of a resident in the global south. Individual actions do matter, such as frequent flying, which has a huge carbon footprint. The term "climate disaster" is used by climate scientists and disaster experts to refer to different scenarios in the context of climate change, which encompasses anything that reduces emissions of planet-warming gases. A shift from coal-fired electricity generation to wind, solar, and gas-powered cars is necessary to avoid catastrophe. Among emergency managers and disaster experts, the term "adaptation" refers to steps aimed at preparing for the current consequences of climate change, which will continue to worsen. Good examples of adaptation include changing how we build houses and roads, and helping people move away from places vulnerable to flooding and wildfires. However, the term "adaptation" is sometimes viewed as a dirty word among environmentalists, as it can imply an admission of failure to cut emissions and an invitation to accept the worsening effects of climate change. Despite this criticism, the need to adapt remains, especially for poorer communities and nations with far less ability to adapt. Nature-based solutions can help address these challenges, using nature to solve human problems, often climate-related ones. For example, meadows and forests act as carbon sinks, keeping greenhouse gases out of the air, while trees can cool cities during heat waves and protect against storms. However, nature-based solutions are also threatened by climate change, as forests face intense wildfires and dying waters. Unless nature-based solutions are combined with drastic reductions in fossil fuel emissions, they risk being hijacked as the ultimate solution to climate change while still relying on fossil fuels. Carbon capture technology aims to trap carbon dioxide emissions from factories and power plants before they escape into the atmosphere, while carbon removal refers to pulling carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, often through natural processes like planting trees. However, technological carbon removal methods, such as direct air capture, are still in development and can be expensive. Scientists argue that carbon removal is necessary to reach net zero emissions and reverse the global warming already caused. This process, sometimes referred to as climate intervention, is controversial, as it raises questions about the potential risks and effects on different parts of the world. Electric vehicles are also part of the climate conversation, as their emissions depend on the local power grid and the environmental impacts of their production. Fuel cell vehicles, powered by hydrogen, also produce emissions, primarily from natural gas. The debate around natural gas is contentious, as it is often marketed as a clean energy source despite being a fossil fuel and a major driver of climate change. Environmental groups have begun to question the labeling of natural gas as clean, as scientific research shows that drilling for gas releases significant amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. The financial sector is also involved, as sustainable investing has grown significantly, with many companies trying to adopt better practices to minimize their impact. Carbon pricing is another approach to addressing climate change, with economists arguing that charging companies and consumers for their emissions provides an incentive to shift toward cleaner energy. There are two main methods of carbon pricing: carbon taxes and cap-and-trade systems. While carbon taxes are often met with political resistance, cap-and-trade systems set a cap on overall emissions and allow for trading permits. Despite the complexities of carbon pricing, it remains a key component of climate policy for many governments, including states like California, which prefer to directly regulate fuel efficiency and mandate renewable energy rather than relying solely on carbon pricing.

The disease has been declared eliminated for years, but cases of a measles outbreak raise questions and answers about everything you want to know. The live weakened form of the measles virus is inside the vaccine, and the virus is grown in a culture of salt and human fetal blood, which helps stabilize the lab-built version of the natural measles virus that acts the way a person gets it from an injection. Children vaccinated receive two doses of the vaccine: the first at months old and the second at years old. Infants months old traveling to the United States or another country should receive one dose of the vaccine beforehand. Adults getting vaccinated is never too late; in fact, with measles occurring in the community, it is a good idea to get vaccinated unless you are sure you previously received two shots of the vaccine. The three diseases the vaccine protects against give lifelong immunity, and a booster dose is never needed. Since the vaccine was made available a decade ago, virtually every child has gotten measles by age. The CDC considers people born before the vaccine was available to be likely to have had measles, while children who received the vaccine should consider getting immunized. One or two vaccines available may be ineffective, but the CDC says the effective vaccine lasts for years; if the vaccine is ineffective, consult your doctor. Nearly all children develop immunity simply by contracting and recovering from the disease, and people getting vaccinated matters. If you are probably thinking about the concept of herd immunity, it means a large number of people are protected from the disease by the vaccine, making the disease less likely and diminishing the risk for unvaccinated people. The threshold for herd immunity varies by disease; for highly contagious diseases, a high percentage of people need to be vaccinated to meet the threshold.

The health law intended to make the individual health insurance market fair and accessible; the Affordable Care Act, passed as law, requires health insurers to sell products to anyone willing to buy, even people with known diseases, which likely means big health care bills. The law also limits how much insurers can vary premiums charged to different people; insurers charge higher prices to older customers, while younger ones face higher prices, and patients with cancer are charged more than healthy ones. The provisions help create healthy customers who buy insurance, with the biggest one being tax credits available on a sliding scale for middle-income Americans. The individual mandate states that anyone who can afford insurance must sign up or face a tax penalty. Fifty years ago, Mao unleashed a decade-long political upheaval intended to transform China, with key events, people, and issues of the Cultural Revolution explained. The Cultural Revolution was a decade-long upheaval with dramatic, often violent effects across China during tumultuous years. The movement fundamentally altered elite politics as Mao tried to control the setting, leading radical youths within the Communist Party to battle perceived enemies among one another. Red Guards were sent to the countryside in the later stages of the Cultural Revolution, targeting people deemed to have ties to the West or the former Nationalist government. Many officials, including future leaders, were eventually killed or committed suicide, leaving a permanent impact. Scholars contend that the trauma of this era contributed to the economic transition in the decades that followed, as the Chinese became willing to embrace market-oriented reforms that spurred growth. This shift took place after the Chinese Communist Central Committee issued outlined ideas for the Cultural Revolution in the months and years leading to Mao's death in September. The subsequent arrest of the Gang of Four, a radical faction of four political leaders including Mao's wife, occurred in October. Although the Cultural Revolution lasted a decade, much of the extreme violence occurred in the first years. The roots of the Cultural Revolution can be traced back to the Great Leap Forward, which resulted in agricultural and industrial output failures that left millions dead, and Mao was partly blamed for sidelining Communist Party leaders who pulled back from extreme efforts.

Inflation, as explained in a FAQ card, represents the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow, typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. Inflation is caused by rising consumer demand, but it can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation can be detrimental, depending on circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a larger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also impacts the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Ransomware virus computer criminals demand money to unlock, becoming a lucrative online scheme; ransomware is expanding in the United States as people fall testament to increasingly targeted methods. Early variations of ransomware locked computers and displayed images, while Russian criminals demanded a fee that was often removed. Current variants target researchers, who say criminals now use internet addresses and notes instead of images. Criminals flash messages to local law enforcement agencies, accusing victims of visiting illegal gambling sites and demanding a fine to unlock their computers. Victims in the United States see messages in English from the FBI and Justice Department, while people in the Netherlands receive similar messages from Dutch local police. Irish variations even demand money, and the latest variants speak to victims through recorded audio messages, telling users to pay within hours or face criminal charges. They even show footage of law enforcement watching. Messages often demand victims buy a card purchased locally and enter a PIN, making it impossible for victims to cancel the transaction. It becomes clear that the criminals' intention is to hunt down and find gangs. Researchers have identified ransomware gangs and tracked one gang that tried to infect a day period, even as researchers track internet addresses, making it difficult to catch those responsible; this requires cooperation among global law enforcement. Criminals are skilled at destroying evidence. Charlie, an independent security researcher based in France, was able to hack one of the computers and discover just one victim from one day last month, accounting for an infection rate of percent attempts and showing that day percent paid in cases. Hackers demanded euros, making a haul from one work.
CDC acknowledges that the coronavirus is infecting others, while Pfizer seeks full FDA approval for its vaccine. The COVID global campaign to vaccinate is likely stalled despite approvals, as evidenced by images of people receiving the vaccine in Pakistan on Wednesday, credited to Ali Agence France Presse/Getty Images. The World Health Organization has approved one Chinese-made COVID vaccine and is expected to approve another soon. The Biden administration is backing intellectual property protections for vaccines to make it easier for countries to vaccinate the world. Experts warn that to reverse the trend, urgent action is needed as the virus spreads rapidly, driven largely by surges in South America and India, and it can no longer spread unchecked. The time for contagious variants to evade protections from vaccines is critical, as rich countries have administered doses to at least one shot of their population, while in Africa, the figure is significantly lower, according to the University of Oxford database. The global vaccination drive has slowed, highlighting the enormous need for vaccines within China and India, the two major manufacturers keeping doses for domestic use. The distribution of vaccines is not only a moral outrage but also economically self-defeating, as the director general told African leaders at a meeting on Saturday. He noted that the gap is tragic, and Friday's approval of the vaccine celebrated by scientists allows for shots to be included in a global initiative to promote equitable vaccine distribution. On Tuesday, millions of doses were shipped, which is less than a quarter of the earlier April target for vaccine access to improve, even for the next week, as another Chinese shot is considered. However, the fanfare is short-lived, as China claims it can make a billion doses by the end of the year, yet Chinese officials say the country is struggling to manufacture enough doses for its population. The pandemic-weary world must keep expectations in check, as this is a golden time for China to practice vaccine diplomacy, but it faces a shortage. A senior fellow at the Global Health Council for Foreign Relations stated that the global access to vaccines is not expected to improve significantly in the coming two to three months due to severe production problems. India, the largest vaccine manufacturer, has only fully vaccinated 5% of its population, and people have been turned away from vaccination centers due to a lack of doses. Giant credit reporting companies keep files on roughly 200 million Americans, and they said Friday they would soon wipe away credit created by certain medical debts. Changes include removing black marks for people who settled debts that went to collections, which cheered consumer advocates and reflected growing acceptance that debts are part of best financial behavior. Companies said the changes would eliminate 70 percent of medical debt accounts from credit reports, which contain data used to calculate the important three-digit credit score key for mortgages, car loans, and rental agreements. Starting in July, medical debts paid that went to collections will no longer appear on credit reports, which currently linger for seven years. New unpaid medical debts will now appear for a full year after being sent to collections instead of the current six months, giving people time to address debt with insurance companies and health care providers. Beginning in the first half of 2024, credit reporting companies said they would exclude unpaid medical collection debts, as the industry remains committed to helping drive fair and affordable access to credit for consumers, according to the chief executives in a statement. These changes mirror actions already taken elsewhere that have been used to generate credit scores, which have already been updated to reduce the influence of paid medical debts in older scoring models. Still, many consumers do not necessarily benefit from these three changes. For example, unpaid medical debts reduce negative information flowing into calculations, and lenders have adopted the latest models. Huge doubt remains, said a staff attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, which helps people with medical debt due to factors like high costs that usually change little. The largest unpaid debts often result from catastrophic illnesses that lead to high bills, even with insurance coverage. The poorest and most vulnerable 20 percent added that a portion of unpaid medical debt accounts remain on credit reports. The widely used credit score changes ignore paid debts and weigh certain unpaid medical collections less heavily. The starting formula found that ignoring collection accounts for medical debts that were otherwise paid actually improves accuracy. It has been eliminated entirely, and it was also found that people with unpaid medical collections are less risky than types of unpaid collections information. People with unpaid accounts, including medical, still face challenges, and none of this goes far enough in eliminating medical debt altogether. One main competitor made similar changes to their formula even earlier, eliminating paid collections, including medical debt, in their scoring model, according to a vice president of scores analytics at the company working with credit reporting companies. These changes shift scores for many people affected, and it is believed that similar effects were seen when reporting companies eliminated two sources of negative information, such as tax liens and civil judgments, which generally saw scores rise by 20 points or less. Consumers otherwise saw their credit reports eliminate medical bills, paid or unpaid, boosting scores by 20 points. Higher scores indicate a better file, and taking away negative information can increase scores. These announcements came just weeks after the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau said it would scrutinize the credit treatment of medical debt and consider an outright ban, including medical debt on credit reports. The agency's research suggested roughly 43 million people have medical bills on their credit reports, with around $58 billion in collections debt appearing on credit reports tied to medical bills. The bureau estimated that medical debts are often difficult to resolve given the insurance system's practices, and sometimes consumers are not even aware of unpaid bills on their credit reports, which can apply to loans and result in lower scores. Regulators targeted medical debts on credit reports seven years ago, and credit reached a settlement with the New York State Attorney General and later attorneys general from dozens of other states to overhaul their approach to fixing errors in the treatment of medical debt. The agreement established a six-month waiting period for reporting medical debt to credit files and also removed medical debts from reports once paid by insurance.

COVID is prompting employers to consider remote arrangements, as employment among adults with disabilities has soared in a tight labor market that opens new doors. "On bad days, I just pick up my laptop and work from home," said workers with disabilities who have long seen fortunes flow with the economy. Federal law prohibits employers from discriminating against people with disabilities and requires them to make reasonable accommodations, but research found that discrimination remains common. One study found that job applications that disclosed a disability were 30 percent less likely to receive interest from prospective employers. Even when they find jobs, workers with disabilities frequently encounter barriers to success, such as bathroom doors that do not open without assistance and hostile work environments. Workers with disabilities, like other groups, face obstacles to employment, and those with criminal records tend to benefit disproportionately in strong job markets where employers have the incentive to seek talent quickly. However, opportunities can quickly dry up, and in the last recession, disabled people were often among the last hired and the first fired, said Adam, chief economist at the Economic Innovation Group, a Washington research organization. Remote work, however, has the potential to break this cycle, as a new study found that employment has risen for workers with disabilities across industries, with the labor market improving in a manner consistent with usual patterns. This improvement has been especially rapid in industries where remote work is common. Many economists believe that the shift toward remote work, unlike the red-hot labor market, is likely to prove lasting, with 31 percent of disabled Americans aged 18 to 64 in jobs as of September, compared to 19 percent just before the pandemic, a record high since the government began tracking employment among adults without disabilities. Employment rates have just returned to pre-pandemic levels, but adults with disabilities have seen their employment rates recover much faster. This is good news, but it is important to understand whether this is a temporary trend or a permanent change. In conclusion, it appears to be a permanent change, as the pandemic has repeatedly forced employers to let workers with disabilities, including those with chronic disorders whose symptoms include pain and severe fatigue, work from home, despite requests often being denied.

Times reconstructed the death of George Floyd using security footage, witness videos, and official documents that show a series of actions by officers that turned fatal. George Floyd was killed in police custody on Monday evening in Minneapolis after police responded to a call about a man allegedly using a counterfeit bill to buy cigarettes. Minutes later, the man was found lying on the ground and pronounced dead shortly thereafter. The 46-year-old George Floyd, originally from Houston, had lost his job at a restaurant when the coronavirus pandemic hit. The crowd's demand for justice for his death triggered major protests in Minneapolis and sparked outrage across the country. One of the officers involved, Derek Chauvin, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder, while three other officers were charged with aiding the murder. Times analyzed bystander videos, security camera footage, and police audio, and spoke with witnesses as experts reviewed documents released by authorities to build a comprehensive picture to better understand how George Floyd died in police custody. The events began with Floyd sitting in a blue car across the street from a convenience store called Cup Foods. Footage from the restaurant's security camera helps understand what happens next. Notably, the camera captured minutes of footage where two employees from Cup Foods confronted Floyd about the alleged counterfeit bill he just used to buy cigarettes, demanding he return the cigarettes. He walked away empty-handed, and four minutes later, a call was made to the police. According to the transcript, the employee says Floyd used fake bills to buy cigarettes. Control soon shifted as the first police vehicle arrived at the scene, with officers Thomas Lane and Alexander Kueng stepping out of the car to approach Floyd's vehicle. Seconds later, Lane pulled out his gun and ordered Floyd to put his hands on the wheel. Lane's gun was pointed back and forth at Floyd, who was filmed by a man in a car parked behind the officers with his hands behind his back as he walked toward the restaurant wall. The transcript now reveals three important facts: first, the police believed they were responding to a man who was drunk and out of control; second, even though the police were expecting a volatile situation, Floyd did not act violently; and third, Floyd seemed to be in distress six minutes into the arrest. Two officers moved Floyd back to the police vehicle, and as they approached the car, they saw Floyd fall to the ground. According to criminal complaints filed, Floyd said he refused to enter the police car, and there was a struggle as he appeared to turn his head to address the officers multiple times, telling them he couldn't breathe. Nine minutes into the arrest, a third police car arrived at the scene carrying officers, including Derek Chauvin, who had previous records of complaints against him and had been sued for throwing a man to the ground and hitting him. Chauvin was involved in three police shootings, one of which was fatal. Chauvin became involved in the struggle to get Floyd into the car, and security camera footage from Cup Foods shows Floyd struggling as Chauvin pulled him back onto the street. Floyd was now lying on the pavement face down, and two witnesses began filming almost simultaneously. The footage from the first witness shows four officers gathered around Floyd, and for the first time, we can clearly see Floyd's face on the ground with three officers applying pressure to his neck and legs. We hear a voice for the first time in the video as Lane appears to tell the person filming to walk away to the sidewalk. On one side, officers radioed a non-emergency medical assistance call, reporting an injury. In the background, we can hear Floyd struggling to call for help, which was quickly upgraded to an emergency medical assistance call. Another bystander, a 16-year-old, filmed from a different angle, and despite calls for medical help, Chauvin kept Floyd pinned for another seven minutes. It is unclear whether Lane was still applying pressure to Floyd as the officer told the bystander to stop filming. In the two videos, Floyd can be heard telling the officers that he can't breathe at least five times in less than five minutes. A bystander noted that Chauvin never took his knee off Floyd, who, with his eyes closed, appeared unconscious. According to medical policing experts, the four police officers committed a series of actions that violated policies, and the case turned fatal as they kept Floyd lying face down while applying pressure for at least five minutes. The combined actions likely restricted his chest, making it impossible for him to breathe. Chauvin's knee on Floyd's neck was a move banned by police departments, as the Minneapolis Police Department policy states that an officer should take action to treat someone even if medical assistance is called. Officers Lane asked twice to roll Floyd onto his side, but Chauvin refused. Twenty minutes into the arrest, the ambulance arrived at the scene, while bystanders checked Floyd's pulse, but Chauvin kept his knee on Floyd's neck for almost another whole minute, even though Floyd appeared to be completely unresponsive. Witnesses reported that Chauvin kept his knee on Floyd's neck for eight minutes. According to a review of video evidence, Floyd was loaded into the ambulance, which left the scene, possibly with a crowd forming and calling for additional medical help. The fire department engine arrived, but officers did not provide clear information about Floyd's whereabouts, according to the fire department incident report, which delayed their ability to help. Meanwhile, Floyd was going into cardiac arrest, and it took the engine five minutes to reach Floyd, who was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital. Two official apps, Pass NYC and COVID Safe, let users show COVID vaccine proof. The NYC Pass is a New York vaccine passport app that launched on March first as a government-issued vaccine passport app for the country. Applications from the city and state vaccination records have allowed millions of New Yorkers to print a pass since its debut, according to the state department of health. To get the pass, users can download it from Apple and Android app stores. The app finds the official record for people vaccinated in New York State and issues a pass containing a unique code certifying they are vaccinated. This code is generated days after a person is fully vaccinated and can be stored on their phone or printed. To find a vaccination record, the app checks the name, date of birth, and code against the county vaccination records. If nearly all information matches the vaccination agency's entry, it can even generate a pass. However, 40 percent of users who tried to get passes in the opening months were unable to, the state said. If users want to find their vaccination record, they can use the city app instead of carrying around a card. The NYC COVID Safe app allows people to show a photo of their vaccination card for either the first dose or two doses of the vaccine as proof of vaccination. One dose or two doses of the vaccine are sufficient to meet the new mandate, though it offers a fraction of the protection gained from getting both doses.

People are less likely to marry if they grow up in certain places, especially liberal ones, as their hometown affects their chances of marriage. Places that make people married at a younger age are less likely, and the place they grow up affects their future income. A large new data set shows a striking pattern in marriage and many issues today, including a partisan divide. Spending childhood nearly anywhere in blue America, especially liberal areas like New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Boston, and Washington, makes people percentage points less likely to marry relative to the rest of the country. Places that encourage marriage are quite like the conservative Mountain West, especially heavily populated areas like Utah, southern Idaho, and parts of Colorado. The conclusions are based on the analysis of data compiled by a team of Harvard economists studying upward mobility and housing tax policy. Economists believe they have identified the role geography plays in people's lives, as data covering five million people who moved as children suggests that children who move from places like Idaho to Chicago become less likely to marry. Even the numbers explain exactly why these patterns exist. The findings of the study focusing on upward mobility encourage exploration of married life in New York, and the effect highlighted in counties around the New York area shows that places that discourage marriage tend to be cities, including San Francisco, Philadelphia, and New Orleans, as well as surrounding areas nationwide. The jurisdiction with the single largest marriage effect is the Washington-New York area, which stands even at the top of the list of the largest counties for marriage. Researchers think they are capturing the effect of children moving from New York, as those who do become less likely to marry. The study analyzed five million people who moved as children, finding that those who moved to New York are indeed less likely to marry compared to otherwise similar people who grew up elsewhere. Younger children who moved to New York are less likely to marry, and one statistic analyzed the odds of being married at a certain age. Researchers asked whether the differences in marriage were much smaller in comparisons, suggesting that childhood experiences make marriage less likely, which seems to simply delay marriage. Researchers found similar patterns when looking at data from places that made marriage likely, which also tended to make marriage likely at a younger age for children. Yet, the conclusions about age are still beyond the best guess for now. The differences in timing for children growing up in New York among places appear to make them less likely to be married. The likelihood of being married is probably less in blue America, and the marriage effects are influenced by presidential voting patterns. A circle represents one county, with circles sized by population based on the share of two-party vote estimates from full childhood in that county. One striking relationship found in the data is that political ideology has a strong effect on marriage; counties that voted Republican in elections generally encourage marriage. This is especially true in rural areas leaning Republican, which promotes marriage, although metropolitan counties that voted Republican tend to turn into marriage-encouraging places like Phoenix, Salt Lake City, and Fort Worth. Polling data tells the story of partisanship and marriage attitudes, as a Pew Research Center survey asked last year whether society is better when people make marriage and children a priority. Sixty percent of Republicans, a group that includes people who lean Republican, said yes, while only twenty-five percent of Democrats shared that view. The attitudes affect children growing up in different places, and it's worth noting that the data set suggests the environment affects later marriage patterns. An experiment known as housing opportunity showed that poor children who moved to less poor neighborhoods at a young age became more likely to marry as adults, similar to children who grew up in poorer areas. The complicated South presents a complex picture, as affluent children tend toward marriage while lower-income children move away. In comparison, the Northeast generally sees marriage rates among children that correlate with income levels. The Mountain West encourages children from lower-income levels, and race certainly plays a role, as lower-income children in the South are disproportionately Black, and marriage rates are also lower among African Americans. The data suggests that race is a factor, as poor families moving to the South see their children become less likely to marry. This evidence effect is restricted to one race, considering mostly white counties in northern Mississippi, just miles south of Memphis. One of the largest class differences shows that rich areas are among the best places in the country for making marriage likely, while poor areas are among the worst. The small-town effect and politics create a dividing line, as less densely populated places seem to promote marriage even when taking political factors into account. Two states that make marriage significantly more likely voted Democratic: Iowa and Oregon, while two states with much lower populations are California and Illinois, with New Jersey and New York being blue states. Rural areas and small towns encourage marriage, as Pew analysis similarly found that the five states with the highest share of men currently married are at least seventy percent Republican: Idaho, Kansas, Utah, Nebraska, and Iowa. None of these states are especially urban, but Utah is worth special attention as it surprisingly leads the nation in encouraging marriage, being home to a large population known for being young. In Austria, the conservative party won a significant percent of the vote in the recent election, giving it the largest bloc in the national parliament, while almost as many people voted for the insurgent far right Freedom Party, which benefited from a strong performance in a social media campaign focused on limiting immigration, lowering taxes, and strengthening the social welfare system. The likely youngest leader in Europe is set to form a coalition with the Freedom Party, led by the Christian Freedom Party, which seeks to curb immigration, particularly from the Middle East, and shrink welfare benefits without curtailing calls for political Islam in the country. The Freedom Party has expressed a desire to leave the European Union despite strong criticism regarding its handling of refugees and borders. As a right-leaning coalition forms in Austria, it joins Hungary and Poland in demanding that the European Union pursue tougher policies on migration, supporting the recent rise of far right parties. The Freedom candidate lost the presidential election in December to independent candidate Alexander Van der Bellen, head of the conservative party, according to Reuters. In Germany, the far right Alternative for Germany party, known as AfD, started four years ago as a protest movement against the euro currency and won a notable percent in the latest election, becoming the third strongest party, marking the first time in years that a far right party has moved into the federal parliament. The party is the fastest growing and has attracted voters disillusioned with the establishment, being anti-European and anti-everything that has been regarded as the norm, according to a former leader of the party who stated that border guards need to turn guns on anyone crossing the frontier illegally. Their policy platform includes calls to ban the construction of mosques. In the Netherlands, the anti-European Union and anti-Islam party Freedom led by Geert Wilders failed to win the March election, finishing in second place, which was a setback for the party that had been leading in the polls and was predicted to gain five seats from the last election. The party also succeeded in pushing many right-leaning parties to adopt tougher immigration policies, likely influencing the policies of the new government. A new right wing party, the anti-European Union Forum for Democracy, won two seats, while one prominent far right politician stated that he wants to ban and close mosques and Islamic schools and was convicted in December for inciting discrimination leading to an anti-immigrant chant at a political rally, with a Dutch court imposing a punishment in February for describing immigrants in the country. In Poland, the right wing Law and Justice party roared back to government, winning a significant percent of the national vote in parliamentary elections in mid-December, while the largest opposition party, Civic Platform, occupied parliament to protest plans to limit news access to the legislative body. Tens of thousands of protesters attended a rally in October against proposed laws that would make virtually all abortions illegal, and the Law and Justice party backed away from these initiatives after a month of effort. The former prime minister Donald Tusk of the Civic Platform party was denied a second term as president of the European Council, while the party's efforts fell flat, with a banner showing the Law and Justice party leader at a demonstration for free media in Warsaw in January, according to Reuters. In Hungary, Viktor Orban's right wing party running on a joint list with the Christian Democratic Party won the last two parliamentary elections, worrying many Western leaders about increasingly authoritarian rule. The party also decisively won the voting in the European Parliament, while President Vladimir Putin of Russia visited in February, stating that the anti-Russian stance of the West is hurting the economy. A bill targeting the party proposed promoting prison terms of eight years for certain offenses. There are many ways assumptions about who is going to vote are particularly important in this race; the poll considers different turnout scenarios. The vote turnout in the poll results indicates that people say they are almost certain to vote, while others, types of people who voted, are estimated based on their voting history, which suggests they will vote regardless. People say they will vote, adjusted to past levels, and the types of people who voted include every active registered voter. Scenarios with higher turnout tend to be better for Democrats. The types of people reached even got the turnout exactly right, but the margin of error captures the error in the poll. A version of the perfect random sample of the voting population is that people respond to surveys, which almost always include older, white, educated, politically engaged individuals who do not accurately represent everyone. Successful outreach to different kinds of voters is called a viewed success rate goal for older males and females, both white and non-white. Cell pollsters compensate by giving weight to respondents that represent groups by age, party registration, gender, likelihood of voting, race, education, and region, mainly using data from voting records and files compiled from a nonpartisan voter file. This works to weight the right categories to know the composition of the electorate. Many pollsters weight education and Hillary's standing results in common ways, while different schemes in the poll result weight party registration. Public polls weight using census data instead of voting records, and like public polls, they weight education. Many polls estimate just one candidate leads in different scenarios, which means much to represent the full range of possible scenarios, let alone the full range of possible election results.

The move effectively creates a new federal agency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Food and Drug Administration, under the Biden administration's division, which will broadly oversee pandemic responses, as stated by Dawn, the Assistant Secretary for Response at the Department of Health and Human Services, credited to Greg Agence France Presse via pool via Getty Images. The Biden administration is creating a new division within the Department of Health and Human Services to coordinate the response to pandemic threats and health emergencies, recognizing that the department is equipped to handle disasters like the coronavirus pandemic. This change, announced internally on Wednesday, will elevate the existing Office of the Assistant Secretary for Response, known as the Operating Division, to a strategic response role. The move effectively creates a new federal agency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Food and Drug Administration, responsible for crucial health logistics, including oversight of the Strategic National Stockpile, emergency medical reserve contracting, and distributing vaccines in emergencies, aiming to increase authority and consolidate powers to operate alongside the CDC, FDA, and National Institutes of Health to manage various aspects of emergency response. It will also create tensions among agencies and campuses outside Washington, as the new division will operate from headquarters in the capital. This change allows for a mobilized coordinated national response to quickly address future disasters and emergencies with greater hiring and contracting capabilities. Dawn, the Assistant Secretary for Response, wrote to employees in a Wednesday email announcing the change, which was first reported by the Washington Post. The surface office division may seem like a Washington bureaucratic move, but people familiar with the change say the new division will build on the work of the Response Office, which already has capabilities built during the pandemic, putting it in charge of the national stockpile, previously run by the CDC, which bitterly opposed the move. The stockpile is short on basic supplies, including ventilators, masks, and protective gear, and stands today as a searing example of failures in the early response. The office already oversees the Advanced Research and Development Authority, responsible for developing innovative vaccines, thrust into the spotlight when President Donald Trump fired the director at the start of the pandemic. The Assistant Secretary running it lacked the capability to contract with companies to purchase vaccines and was forced to rely on the Department of Defense to handle purchasing and distribution of shots. The office, now an operating division, will enable the taking of responsibilities, according to people familiar with the move. The new hiring and contracting authority will be outlined in a memo, and the newer overseeing of the national stockpile will limit typical staff decisions, which appeared to catch top federal health officials by surprise, including those at the White House and CDC. Senior officials said Lawrence, a former CDC adviser who directs the Institute for National and Global Health Law at Georgetown University, indicated that the announcement on Wednesday was a little vague and makes it seem as if one agency is badly needed to handle key functions of another agency, even raising concerns about the consequences of this shift. The Biden administration and future administrations will need to address this, as a spokeswoman for the CDC said the agency is supportive of the Assistant Secretary's vision and is a critical partner in addressing public health, continuing to work closely together to advance and protect the health of the American people. A spokeswoman for the former acting chief scientist at the FDA and a National Security Council official commented that the office was always meant to be a strategic arm of the federal health bureaucracy, but there is a need to be careful that the new entity becomes operational without creating confusion about the CDC's essential response role.

His dad made the ascent together as they climbed the trail in a national park, a path with steep sides and signs warning of death that convinced them to turn around halfway, resting beyond a dizzying drop overlooking green Maine and the blue Atlantic Ocean. With a slight strain in each step, Andy was ready to move, while his dad stood with his hat backward and shirt still damp, catching his breath. "I think we need a water break," he said, looking at Andy. "I think so too," Andy replied. Their relationship had been complicated; one of his childhood memories was of a Saturday morning when they had to stop soon to order an exact meal that took patient guidance and care. The trail stood in stark contrast to the frustrated childhood cries during long, steep hills, where they would stop to listen and encourage each other, feeling comfortable and secure. But as Andy grew older, things changed; his dad lost his job, fell into depression, and became absent, which made it hard for Andy to understand him. Despite dealing with mental illness, his dad became critical of his flaws and shortcomings. Andy lost his glasses and got asked at the grocery store about names for family dinner, sitting largely silent until interrupted by unrelated questions. He promised himself he would never make himself vulnerable like that again, never sharing past regrets or failures. His dad, who scaled the trail with much ease initially, walked ahead carrying the pack. Andy checked his thoughts as he saw the man sitting, breathing slowed, and asked, like many times before, if he had read David's column that week filled with discussions on the necessity of the democratic process. He felt guilt—guilt of superiority, guilt of ever buying into standards that imagined what a proper man meant. On the trail, he realized he was never dealing with setbacks or losing footing; the way he looked at his dad showed he knew employment was about getting the right type of grocery store job. He saw his dad as a man measuring himself against external standards, while his childhood self felt supported by his father on the mountain. This transition was an external one, a passage through a singular circumstance that forced him to become a man rather than sitting at the cliff. His father wondered if maybe it simply meant looking beyond, and without hesitation, his dad's willingness to get back up was the best example of a man. As he finished his thoughts, Brooks' article reminded him to breathe and still get water, reaching back into his pack.

The department is now adapting to the rise in crime since the beginning of the year, as Ashley observed that at the start of the year, crime began to rise in several categories, with June seeing a significant uptick. Archived recordings show that the NYPD is investigating spree shootings during the first official weekend of summer, with a dozen people shot from Friday night into Saturday morning. Ashley mentioned that the trend seems to be accelerating, with nine victims fatally shot tonight across four locations, and deadly shootings began just this morning in Brooklyn, continuing throughout the day in Manhattan, the Bronx, and Staten Island. As the month ends, shootings are up compared to last year, with sirens still ringing five months later. Michael Barbaro acknowledged that behind the numbers, there is nothing but conversation about living in New York. Ashley remarked that five blocks from the hospital is part of the soundtrack of everyday life. Michael Barbaro pointed out that the increase in shootings and murders raises questions about the causes, suggesting that many people instinctively think it is somehow related to the moment of forceful rejection of policing that occurred during protests in response to police actions. Ashley noted that while it may seem obvious, the situation is much more complex, with three big theories emerging. One consensus is that the pandemic has exacerbated longstanding problems of gun violence, particularly unemployment, as many people are losing jobs and sinking deeper into poverty, which creates greater desperation. Additionally, there is a proliferation of illegal guns in New York City, complicating the situation. Michael Barbaro asked how this relates to the police's presence, and Ashley explained that the pandemic led to officers being removed from duty due to the virus, with thousands of officers calling in sick every day at the height of the pandemic, nearly a percent of the force. Michael Barbaro expressed surprise, and Ashley elaborated that the absence of officers on the street likely contributed to the rise in violence, as a police presence can deter crime. She emphasized that when an officer is present, the likelihood of someone getting shot decreases. Michael Barbaro noted that investigations by police detectives often come to a halt when officers get sick, as one shooting often leads to another, whether it is a rival shooting or someone seeking revenge. Ashley reiterated that the first theory is that the pandemic is fueling shootings, as officers who could potentially prevent them are absent. The second theory relates to the protests that erupted following George Floyd's death in police custody in Minneapolis, which led to a significant political response and demands for police reform. Ashley explained that the police were initially deployed to manage protests and rampant looting, which meant fewer officers were available for investigating shootings. Michael Barbaro asked how the protests play into this theory, and Ashley responded that the political response to the protests has included changes to anti-crime units, which are traditionally responsible for getting guns off the streets of New York City. She explained that anti-crime officers have become controversial due to their tactics, which often involve stopping cars and searching individuals without explanation, leading to tension between police and communities of color. Archived recordings indicate that the anti-crime unit has been effective but has also been involved in many police shootings. Michael Barbaro pointed out that the decision to pull the plug on the anti-crime unit was a significant move, and Ashley noted that it reflects a cultural struggle within the police department about how to balance crime control with community relations. She expressed concern that removing anti-crime officers from the streets and publicly announcing a shift in policy might embolden people to carry guns, which could lead to increased violence. Michael Barbaro acknowledged that the second theory centers around the protests and the political response to them, which has created a level of mistrust between police and communities that have historically experienced aggressive policing. Ashley emphasized that this mistrust complicates police work, as people in these communities may be less likely to cooperate with investigations, making it harder to solve crimes and leading to a cycle of violence. Michael Barbaro noted that the police's response to the protests may also be affecting their behavior on the streets, as officers may be hesitant to engage in situations where violence could escalate. Ashley agreed, stating that officers may feel that intervening in certain situations could jeopardize their careers and family support. Michael Barbaro asked about the police's perspective regarding the demands for budget cuts and reform, and Ashley explained that there seems to be a sense among officers that the public wants to abolish the police, which influences their willingness to engage in proactive policing. Michael Barbaro questioned whether these reforms were indeed responsible for the increase in crime, and Ashley pointed out that the bail law passed last year was intended to address systemic inequities in the justice system but has been criticized for allowing individuals to return to the streets before facing trial. Archived recordings show that the commissioner believes that judges should make common-sense decisions regarding bail, especially for individuals deemed dangerous to the community. Ashley explained that the second part of this theory involves measures taken to slow the spread of COVID-19 in jails and prisons, which also led to the release of violent offenders back onto the streets. Michael Barbaro noted that the argument is that these individuals are involved in the current surge of shootings and murders. Ashley emphasized that the data does not support a direct link between bail reform and rising crime, citing critics like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who have released data showing that most individuals committing crimes were not released due to bail reform. She argued that the current economic desperation and unemployment levels are significant factors contributing to the rise in crime. Michael Barbaro acknowledged that the situation is complex, with multiple factors at play, including the pandemic and protests, which have exacerbated existing issues. Ashley concluded by stating that while policing and reforms are part of the solution, they are not the only factors that need to be addressed to effectively tackle rising crime rates.
