Six systems North Korea needs to master to achieve its long-sought goal of being able to reliably hit the United States. North Korea can actually hit the United States with a nuclear weapon, according to the Japan Broadcasting Corporation. North Korea is speeding toward a goal sought for decades: the ability to hit a major American city with a nuclear weapon. Actually striking the United States would provide a suicide capability to help North Korea deter invasion and wield increased global influence. American intelligence agencies estimate North Korea will reach this milestone next year, and experts think it is already reliably sending a nuclear warhead halfway around the globe. Extremely difficult challenges remain, as the systems North Korea needs to advance and master to reach the mainland are probably already possible. An intercontinental ballistic missile looks like the least complex option, as experts best determine the main engine fuel, guidance, bomb steering engines, and the warhead. The main engine, bomb fuel, and guidance systems are critical, with many years of empty claims and abandoned models. North Korea tested its missile twice in July, and the second test appeared capable of reaching the West Coast, including Chicago and Denver, also potentially extending its range. The program has long been known for modest strides and spectacular failures, but analysts say a powerful new main engine lies behind these advances, calling it stronger and more reliable than past models. The range of North Korea's missile tests in July indicates that the vehicle can survive entry, and a crude version could be ready next year. It is relatively easy to get a vehicle into space, but the main problem is developing a missile warhead that can withstand the fiery heat and great violence of atmospheric entry. North Korea's launch targets include Japan and China, as well as the United States, with the entry atmosphere presenting challenges. The intercontinental ballistic missile falls back to Earth at speeds of roughly four miles per second, and intense friction through the thick blanket of air produces waves of heat that can badly engineer the warhead. Long before hitting the target, the direction of travel is affected by atmospheric forces and intense heat. One trick for designers is to use thick materials that burn evenly, making a shield that sends dangerous heat away. Manufacturing errors can produce uneven burns that throw the warhead off course. Last month, a camera in Japan caught a glimpse of a North Korean warhead in the atmosphere at night, first looking like a shooting star before leaving a bright trail and disappearing. Experts see video evidence of the vehicle breaking into pieces, but others, including Joshua, an editor, say the quality of the video is poor and it is difficult to determine what happened. This break could mean anything, but it is clear that North Korea is trying hard and making progress. Military intelligence experts tend to assume the worst, which is arguably the approach to weapons of mass destruction. North Korea keeps up the rate of missile tests, likely developing a crude entry vehicle that it could possess next year. Private analysts say that making a bomb fit for a missile has probably already been completed, with much technical debate surrounding the North Korean threat. The question has turned to whether nuclear arms can fit inside the cramped space of a missile nose; the first bomb was five feet wide, while last year North Korea released a photo of its leader, Kim Jong-un, with a bomb described as meant to fit a missile warhead that is two feet wide. It is small enough to be a trick, as shown in a photo from the United States Department of Energy. It is impossible to know whether the photo shows a working weapon, but nuclear experts, including American intelligence agencies, judge that North Korea has indeed succeeded in making nuclear arms small enough to fit atop a missile. The country has conducted five nuclear tests, which probably means it has developed smaller, lighter bombs that can travel farther. Estimates suggest that the range of North Korea's missiles increases dramatically with the weight of the warhead, with North Korean missiles potentially reaching New York, San Diego, San Francisco, and Seattle. The accuracy of North Korea's missile tests in July indicates that the vehicles can hit targets within roughly three to five miles, but true accuracy is impossible to determine, as they usually fall into the sea outside intended targets. Experts know little about the intended targets, and even good enough aiming at a city may be insufficient to reliably hit hardened targets like military installations. Analysts say North Korea appears to be working toward accurate designs, but currently, it seems to use blunt entry vehicles that are relatively easy to make but slower and less accurate than advanced models. Blunt designs can make powerful bombs, and on Sunday, North Korea conducted an underground nuclear test that clearly demonstrated the destructive power of bombs dropped on Japanese cities during World War II. Early analysis indicated that the blast was roughly four times stronger than the bombs dropped on Japan, raising the destructive power while keeping the bomb relatively small. Adding fuel to the bomb presents technically daunting steps to produce weapons with times the destructive power of known bombs. North Korea's test bomb was mounted, and photographs released showed a new weapon, but it is unclear whether the test actually involved a bomb or was a somewhat modest advance achieved using a smaller amount of fuel to boost a less powerful atomic bomb. A rough map shows the difference in destruction between a bomb that is one times stronger and one of the largest ever deployed, hitting the center of Los Angeles. The strength of the bomb would cause widespread fatalities and severe burns in the surrounding areas. North Koreans have shown great interest in making bombs, and experts have a clear sense of how far they have traveled on this road. The clearest indication of a large underground nuclear blast far north detonated is that nothing comes even close to getting past United States defenses. Nobody knows for sure if Americans can just shoot down an incoming nuclear warhead with a missile, but the protection has never been used. Highly choreographed tests often fail to hit speeding targets, and the Department of Defense's missile defense agency plays a numbers game. If North Korea fires three nuclear missiles at the United States and manages to shoot down two, it still accomplishes much of its objective with just one destruction. North Korea is clearly exploring ways to improve its defenses and likely investigates others, as it simultaneously fired four missiles in March to make it harder for American defenses to shoot down incoming systems. Following the two weeks of images from the protests in Ferguson, police officers deployed military gear and equipment to quell unrest, while President Obama ordered a review of several federal programs to provide money and equipment to local police. The flow of money and equipment to local police comes from homeland security grants, which were created and expanded after the attacks in September, spurring the creation of several federal programs that grant money to states for equipment and training related to anti-terrorism strategies. The two largest programs in recent years have been a significant source of funds for local and state law enforcement, with federal grants allocating billions in the fiscal year for the Urban Areas Security Initiative and the State Homeland Security Program. The State Homeland Security Program and the Urban Areas Security Initiative allocate money to states based on population, with program proposals using a formula that sets a minimum for states to distribute funds to local areas. Missouri received nearly $10 million, which is the median amount received by states per capita, making it the fifth lowest amount of money granted. Dozens of high-risk metro areas share funds with surrounding counties, and the St. Louis metro area received $1 million, significantly less than larger cities like New York ($50 million), Chicago ($30 million), Los Angeles ($20 million), and Washington ($15 million). Since St. Louis County spent $1 million of its portion of the awards on equipment, including armored trucks and helicopters, the county mostly used the grant for protective gear like ballistic suits and bomb tools. The Justice Department grants, particularly the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant Program, serve as the largest source of Justice Department funding for state and local law enforcement, although congressional financing for the program has fallen in recent years to $1 billion per year from late 2000s levels. Recipients use grants for policing programs, training, and equipment, unlike the Department of Homeland Security grants, which also fund personnel increases and weapon purchases. Researchers measured the impact on transmission among participants every week, seeking to detect signs of the virus, and found a 67 percent reduction in positive cases among the vaccinated. These encouraging results lend support to the strategy deployed in Britain and other countries to prioritize providing as many first doses of vaccines as possible, setting aside concerns about people getting their second doses later than initially planned. The latest data is bearing on the debate over whether to space doses of the two vaccines authorized in the United States, Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, since the data on candidate vaccines has led scientists to call for the United States to follow the lead of Britain and other countries that opted to delay second doses of vaccines by weeks. The vaccine appeared effective with two shots, longer than the originally intended four-week gap. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers found that among clinical trial participants who received two standard strength doses at least three months apart, the vaccine was 82 percent effective, compared to 54 percent effective for doses given less than six weeks apart. The vaccination strategy of spacing doses by three months is necessary due to limited vaccine supplies in the short term, as researchers wrote in a newly released paper that builds on data issued late last year, which found the vaccine to be 76 percent effective when given in two standard strength doses. Initial findings indicated that the efficacy was much higher at 90 percent for the first dose of the vaccine given at half strength. The Oxford AstraZeneca researchers initially attributed the different levels of effectiveness to the lower strength of the initial dose but gradually reached the conclusion that the amount of time between doses is likely the explanation. The disease has been declared eliminated for years, but cases of measles outbreaks raise questions and answers about everything you want to know. The vaccine contains a weakened form of the measles virus, which is grown in a culture of salt and human fetal blood, and this helps stabilize the lab-built version of the natural measles virus. This acts the way a person gets the injection, and children are vaccinated with two doses of the vaccine: the first at months old and the second at years old. Infants months old traveling to the United States or another country should receive one dose of the vaccine beforehand. Adults can get vaccinated; it is never too late. In fact, with measles occurring in the community, it is a good idea to get vaccinated unless you are sure you have previously received two shots of the vaccine. The three diseases the vaccine protects against provide lifelong immunity, and a booster dose is never needed. For the past decade, virtually every child has received the measles vaccine by age, and the CDC considers people born before 1957 likely immune to measles. Children who received the vaccine should consider getting immunized again, as one or two vaccines may be ineffective. The CDC states that the effective vaccine lasts for years, but one vaccine may not be sufficient, so it is important to consult a doctor. Many children develop immunity simply by contracting and recovering from the disease, and people getting vaccinated is crucial. If you are probably thinking about the concept of herd immunity, it means that a large number of people are protected from the disease through vaccination, making the disease less likely to spread and diminishing the risk for unvaccinated individuals. The threshold for herd immunity varies by disease, and for highly contagious diseases, a high percentage of people need to be vaccinated to meet this threshold.

Times reconstructed the death of George Floyd through security footage, witness videos, and official documents that show a series of actions by officers that turned fatal. The video contains scenes of graphic violence as George Floyd was killed in police custody on Monday evening in Minneapolis. Police responded to a call about a man allegedly using a fake bill to buy cigarettes, and minutes later, they arrived to find him lying on the ground, pronounced dead shortly after. The 46-year-old George Floyd, originally from Houston, lost his job at a restaurant when the coronavirus pandemic hit. The crowd's demand for justice for his death triggered major protests in Minneapolis and sparked outrage across the country. One of the officers involved, Derek Chauvin, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder, while three other officers were charged with aiding the murder. Times analyzed bystander videos, security camera footage, police audio, and witness statements, and experts reviewed documents released by authorities to build a comprehensive picture to better understand how George Floyd died in police custody. Events begin with Floyd sitting in a blue car across the street from a convenience store called Cup Foods. The footage from the restaurant's security camera helps to understand what happens next. Note that the camera footage shows two employees of Cup Foods confronting Floyd about the alleged bill he just used to buy cigarettes, demanding the cigarettes back as he walks away empty-handed. Four minutes later, a call to the police is made, and according to the transcript, the employee says Floyd used fake bills to buy cigarettes. Control soon shifts as the first police vehicle arrives at the scene, and officers Thomas Lane and Alexander Kueng step out of the car to approach Floyd. Seconds later, Lane pulls out his gun, not knowing exactly how to order Floyd to put his hands on the wheel. As Lane's gun is pointed at Floyd, he moves back and forth, and a man filming the confrontation from a car parked behind the officers sees Floyd with his hands behind his back walking towards the restaurant wall. According to the transcript, three important facts emerge: first, the police believed they were responding to a man who was drunk and out of control; second, even though the police were expecting a situation, they saw Floyd acted violently; and third, Floyd seemed to be in distress six minutes into the arrest. Two officers move Floyd back to the vehicle, and as the officers approach the car, they see Floyd fall to the ground. According to criminal complaints filed, Floyd says he refuses to enter the police car, and a struggle ensues as he appears to turn his head to address the officers multiple times, according to the complaints, telling them he can't breathe. Nine minutes into the arrest, the third and final police car arrives at the scene, carrying officers Derek Chauvin, who has previous records of complaints brought against him, and was sued for throwing a man to the ground and hitting him. Chauvin is involved in the struggle to get Floyd into the car, and security camera footage from Cup Foods shows Floyd struggling as Chauvin pulls him back from the seat onto the street. The FAQ card states that inflation, which results in the loss of purchasing power over time, means that a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow, typically expressed as an annual change in the prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation are the result of rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise or fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation can be bad, depending on the circumstances, as fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth; inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value to a better extent. The trillion-dollar bill's impact on inflation largely depends on how much the economy changes and whether Americans increase their spending as a result of the legislation; many economists say it will create a short-term stimulus plan, raising money gradually, and Americans are less likely to spend additional dollars quickly. The preferred inflation gauge climbed at the fastest pace in nearly four decades, as the Omicron outlook index hit its highest level in November since earlier that year, with big price increases largely reserved for goods in short supply due to demand surging while shipping lines struggled to keep up; officials expected the situation to sort itself out as the economy reopened and returned to normal. Inflation FAQs indicate that inflation represents a loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that the dollar today is worth less than it was yesterday, typically expressed as an annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise or fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Whether inflation is bad depends on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Recently, price pressures have spread across categories like rent, suggesting that quick overall increases may last longer, as supply chains have gotten worse instead of better. Of course, it has become clear that the road to normalcy is longer and winding, with forecasters counting on the Biden administration to pull through, including increasing the supply of oil and gasoline and trying to keep ports open longer. The effort to clear up much of the job of controlling inflation falls on the central bank, which is in charge of full employment and stable prices. Fed officials are faced with conflicting evidence as they decide whether the economy needs much more help; as the year ends, it is still on a high note with a booming economy. Diane, the chief economist at an accounting advisory firm, noted that Fed officials and economists think price gains will slow from the current rapid pace next year, but nobody is certain how quickly or completely that will happen. The effect of Omicron has provided evidence of a pop in prices, as a related measure, the consumer price index, showed a high report with a rising percent in November, while the closely watched measure called core inflation, which excludes food and fuel volatility, also came in high.

Send the bill to China; it happens when the United States decides on tax tariffs for imported goods. Tariffs work as China sees the bill for imported goods entering the port of the United States. Initially, the bill gets recorded, and tariffs usually raise questions about who pays them. Companies tend to pass the costs onto contracts, and almost always see costs rise when tariffs are imposed on goods. Imports now mean that a company paying, say, a certain percent to bring in the exact product faces a choice: the extra costs of tariffs can either be passed on to American consumers in the form of higher prices or absorbed by the company, particularly in a competitive market where the supply chain can easily move. Washing machines are a good example; prices rose in the United States earlier this year when the administration imposed tariffs. Companies also try to minimize tariffs by switching suppliers or changing the products they sell. In the case of China, tariffs mean moving factories from Beijing to Vietnam. If one company pays tariffs, it can make an end run around American companies by negotiating concessions with the Chinese supplier, likely threatening to shift production. In this case, Chinese profits fall as they bear at least some of the costs of tariffs. Research suggests that American companies are essentially passing the bill back to China, while companies choose to absorb extra costs, accepting lower profits, or choose neither and raise prices immediately. They may also pay to shift production based on the idea of economically efficient pricing. The charge for products has changed with the existence of tariffs. In the case of Apple, they charge a premium for iPhones and decide to accept smaller profit margins, becoming subject to tariffs from China. In the end, they are paying, but never directly. Certainly, there are ways American tariffs hurt Chinese companies, as they move production to Vietnam, leading to less economic growth in China, though there is a direct benefit to American production. It is a short-term headache for companies as they find new factories.

Young children seem to catch and transmit the virus less than adults, but rising numbers of cases, hospitalizations, and deaths show that they are increasingly affected by the coronavirus. Rates are rising fast among children as schools begin in-person classes. Data compiled by the American Academy of Pediatrics this summer shows that cases, hospitalizations, and deaths from coronavirus increased at a faster rate among children and teenagers compared to the general public. This change since August includes hospitalizations and deaths among children, with the source being the American Academy of Pediatrics. The data set from August varies from state to state, possibly due to differences in how the virus affects infants and young children. For example, many states group infants and teenagers into the same category, while one state even includes people up to age 25. The rise remains similar across states, as young children seem to catch and transmit the virus less than adults. Children ages 5 to 17 tend to experience severe complications, Sean, vice chairman of the American Academy's Committee on Infectious Diseases, said. With substantial community spread in many parts of the United States, infections among children are rising. Reported cases come as part of widespread testing, and evidence suggests minors are becoming infected at a higher rate now than earlier in the year. Hospitalizations and deaths among children have increased, although much is still unknown about how the virus affects young people compared to adults. Black and Latino children who contract the virus are likely to be hospitalized. "On the front lines of the pandemic, hospitals tell us they are taking care of lots of kids who are sick," said Sean. "It is less severe for children than for adults." Since the beginning of summer, every state in the country has seen an increase in the number of young people testing positive for coronavirus. A Fed official states that interest rate increases are warranted. Richard, the Federal Vice Chair, said in a speech on Wednesday that the economy meets expectations and thinks it is enough for the Fed to start raising rates by the end of next year. This meaningful statement comes from one of the highest-ranking members of the policy-setting committee. He said that expected inflation will moderate and remain slightly above the percent target of the central bank, which aims to hit or exceed it over time. The unemployment rate is dropping sharply toward the full employment goal, and he believes that the three necessary conditions for raising the target range of the federal funds rate will be met by the end of the year. He discussed inflation in a FAQ card, explaining that inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow. Inflation is typically expressed as an annual change in the prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in limited economic conditions, such as oil production and supply chain problems. While inflation can be bad, it depends on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor particularly hard, as poor households spend a larger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. He noted that the unemployment rate is expected to reach a maximum of around percent by the end of next year, a level that Fed officials projected in June, with the jobless rate currently standing at percent, down from a pandemic peak of much lower percent.

President Biden said Russia is targeting Kyiv, the capital, in the coming week, while the Russian president said earlier Friday that he is still open to diplomacy, citing intelligence. Biden says Putin has decided to invade Ukraine, according to the New York Times Daily today. Officials say Russia will invade Ukraine early next week. Colleague Michael Schwartz traveled to Ukraine to understand how Ukrainians are making sense of this perilous moment. On Tuesday, February, Mike has been in Ukraine for a couple of weeks now and tells us it looks like and feels like right now. Michael Schwartz arrived in Kyiv at the beginning of January, where the noise of military buildup suggests planning for war, yet nothing is happening in the streets; they are quiet, with military vehicles on the street and soldiers. People are lined up to take money and groceries as they arrive in the new place. The story went that he took a walk around town, and at one place he arrived in Kyiv, he wanted to take the pulse of the city in Independence Square, which was fairly empty. He took a walk up the hill behind the square and happened upon a small wooden chapel and a black steel monument with real-life photos of individuals, their names, ages, and cities. This monument commemorates the hundred individuals killed during the heavy shootout several days into the Kyiv uprising, which Ukrainians refer to as the Revolution of Dignity. Michael Schwartz notes that the Revolution of Dignity actually started in the fall of Ukraine, when a sign of association agreement with the European Union was locked in by the country under pressure from Vladimir Putin, the president of Ukraine at the time. What seemed like a pretty minor thing to some Ukrainians felt like a major betrayal, leading to the Kremlin-backed government pouring into the streets to express their anger, resulting in a months-long occupation of Independence Square in central Kyiv. Archived recordings of non-English speech capture the protests where protesters refused to leave the square, and the government slowly lost its grip on the situation. The government ordered riot police forces to open fire on the crowd in an effort to disperse them, killing over a hundred people. At this point in history, the protesters were able to drive the Kremlin-backed government out of Kyiv and install a new government. Ukrainians look back with a great deal of pride at being able to force the numbers to overturn what seemed to be Moscow's control over the country's affairs. 

Michael Schwartz became a site for people around Ukraine to come to memorialize those lost. Two elderly women were cleaning the site when Michael Schwartz approached them and, speaking Russian, asked them to describe the memorial. One turned to him and said it was a memorial for the heroes of Ukraine. Michael Schwartz noted that every time one of the individuals died during the uprising, their birthday hangs with photos in a little holder. It sounds like there is still much pain alive in the moment of Ukrainian society. Michael Schwartz thinks everything has changed, as people witnessed their government firing on children, elderly people, and citizens. People came to express their shock at Russia's actions, which they felt were supportive of the Kremlin. This really changed the way people think about their country. Michael Schwartz encountered a young woman in Independence Square who started speaking Russian but then switched to Ukrainian, indicating that she understood the importance of speaking the national language, especially now during the war between the two countries. 

At least, this shows respect for the country and its language. Mike describes a real kind of turn away from the Russian language, which was a surprise to him. Michael Schwartz found Kyiv to be a place where he expected people to be western-oriented; having traveled and covered this part of the world for years, he knows that Ukraine is complicated, with a push and pull between Ukraine and Russia. On one side, the West considers Ukraine to be western, while on the other side, Russia considers it to be a defining feature of the country since the Soviet collapse. Weighing on his mind are the possible scenarios of a Russian attack on Ukraine, knowing that Putin wants to return Ukraine to his sphere of influence, while the West's willingness to come to the rescue remains a big mystery. 

At this moment, Ukrainians are wondering how they will respond to an attack, whether they will rise up in resistance or accept their fate. Michael Schwartz rented a car in Kyiv and decided to drive south to get outside the city, where the land quickly opens up to brown and green fields stretching for miles. He stopped in a town called an important city where protests had toppled the government in Kyiv. Vladimir Putin struck back in the peninsula, leading to a separatist war in the eastern region of Ukraine. Archived recordings of gunfire capture the tension in the area. Michael Schwartz visited a hospital for rehabilitation of military veterans, where he met a retired sergeant named Alexander, who told his story of beginning to fight in the war in the east. He made an interesting revelation: Alexander was born in Russia but became a Ukrainian soldier fighting against Russian-backed separatists. Michael Schwartz learned that Alexander's family members still live in Russia, and he described a painful moment when he had to confront his aunt, who still lives in Russia, about the war. 

Alexander accused Ukrainians of killing Russians in the street, and Michael Schwartz tried to convince him that it wasn't true, but it strained their relationship to the point where they stopped talking. Alexander described a painful time filled with accusations that were sort of Kremlin propaganda. He recounted a memory of a young soldier he saw having breakfast, who later learned that a year-old soldier's young wife was pregnant and that their small child was killed in battle that morning. Alexander said this is something he will never forget. Importantly, he expressed the emotional journey of being born in Russia and fighting against Russians, losing friends along the way. Michael Schwartz described it as incredibly painful, as Alexander was forced to make a decision about his identity and chose Ukraine. When asked whether he would fight if troops amassed at the border with the threat of war looming, he said yes. 

Michael Schwartz used a metaphor to describe the situation, saying it feels like a giant neighbor is constantly coming into your apartment and ordering you around, trying to throw you out. He traveled across the river to a steel mill built downtown, where he found it interesting that the signs were in Russian. Michael Schwartz wanted to see the factory, which is one of the larger steel factories in Ukraine and a source of pride. The factory was opened at a time when Ukraine was hugely dependent on the Russian market for its goods. The opening of the factory was not just a Ukrainian success story but also a Russian success story, as a large portion of its product was sold to Russia. However, with the war beginning, the town and factory, which are less than miles away from the front border, have sealed their business. The factory's business with Russia has come to an end, and it sounds like this is another break, another change inside Ukraine, both economically and emotionally. 

Nevertheless, it feels like a switch has flipped, and the factory is now looking to do business with Europe instead of Russia. Michael Schwartz spoke with a press woman who described the trauma that Ukrainian businesses are facing as they find ways to develop and improve. He walked onto a mostly frozen river, where he saw a number of men ice fishing. He tried to talk to them, but one dismissed him. He met another man named Viktor, who was dressed from head to toe and came alone to spend days ice fishing. They got to talking and found out that Viktor had served in the Red Army. Michael Schwartz learned that Viktor was born in the Soviet Union and had a much Soviet tradition of thinking. Viktor seemed to believe that Ukraine should remain within the orbit of Russia, even though it is independent. 

He expressed a pro-Russian view, saying he thinks Ukraine should join NATO, a western military alliance, and that Ukraine has chosen a Russian direction over a European one. Viktor spoke of a belief that Russia needs to be put in its place and that if Russia attacks Ukraine, it is almost certain that the Ukrainian response will be to stand and fight. Viktor's perspective is astonishing, as he is a man in his late life who has become opposed to the Soviet mindset, indicating a shift in attitudes. Michael Schwartz thinks fundamentally the question now is really hard to know; soon tanks may start rolling through the streets and rockets may start falling. One thing is clear, though: Ukraine came under attack for the first time when the separatist movement was provoked by the Kremlin, and the Ukrainian military fell apart. The reason Ukraine lost territory was that college students, history professors, and people from across the country joined volunteer equipped companies, like the steel factory he visited, and rose to fight the separatists. This forced Russia to send regular troops and equipment to push back, as half the country was lost. Volunteers appeared almost overnight, and as Michael Schwartz traveled around the country, everyone he talked to, including veterans in rehabilitation hospitals, said they would pick up arms and fight for their lives, their children, and their futures. 

Putin may not fully understand the Ukrainian people, as he assumes they are just like Russians who will accept his rule. This assumption is mistaken. Meanwhile, the State Department announced the relocation of remaining embassy staff from Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, to the western part of the country. Secretary of State Antony Blinken cited the buildup of Russian forces as a reason for this decision.
Time prevents now; countries are trying to seize the moment of the coronavirus. China and other countries struggle to control the spread, as Michael Barbaro of The New York Times reports. Michael Barbaro discusses how China says it has made lifesaving reforms since the last public health crisis years ago, but the deadly coronavirus is spreading rapidly across the country. A colleague reports from the center of the outbreak on Thursday, January first, about how the outbreak started with early reports of a mysterious virus affecting Wuhan city in central China. An archived recording reveals staff at a Wuhan hospital working around the clock to identify the mystery virus, with people falling ill from a pneumonia-like virus that scientists are calling coronavirus. The archived recording indicates that experts believe this new kind of coronavirus typically causes symptoms of the common cold, but in rare cases, it can lead to pneumonia. The frightening virus spreads from animals to humans and is believed to be behind serious respiratory illnesses. It sounded pretty scary, as the official narrative suggested the strain could pass from human to human, but the animals involved were thought to be from a live produce market in Wuhan, where wild animals were sold. At this point, the assumption was that people who came into contact with animals picked up the virus. Michael Barbaro notes that it sounds like the meat market is where the virus passed from animals to humans, which is a pretty small problem at that point. Reports indicate that people were infected and four died. The archived recording features Chinese officials saying the outbreak is under control, but Michael Barbaro is thinking about how he hears the Chinese government talking this way and feels a bit skeptical, knowing the government's history with outbreaks. He recalls reports from international media about the virus spreading and begins to question whether officials are being truthful about what is happening. Michael Barbaro reflects on the history of situations like the SARS outbreak years ago, which turned into a global health crisis that infected thousands and killed many. A big part of the reason it spread violently was that the Chinese government was slow to inform the world. For months, the virus spread rapidly in China while the world just did not know a lot. Given the experience with SARS, many Chinese people are skeptical of anything the government says regarding public health. Michael Barbaro imagines that as a reporter, he feels similarly skeptical and really wants to ensure he gets the story right. He wants to double-check the facts about the small-scale outbreak the government is portraying and talk to people who are getting sick from the virus to get a sense of the severity and whether they are getting the care they need. Michael Barbaro lives in Beijing and rushes to the bureau, grabbing enough masks for the next couple of days before heading to the airport. He remembers that almost everyone on the flight to Wuhan was wearing masks, which struck him as he had never seen people wearing masks on such a scale before. It felt like there was a sense of anxiety already in the air. Even after landing, he rushed to meet an ambulance doctor who was posting on social media about the outbreak, challenging the official narrative. The doctor was saying that he did not believe the official numbers and thought it was another SARS-like outbreak. Michael Barbaro recalls how posts went online but then quickly disappeared, making it clear that the government was cleaning up the internet of critical questions about the official data. He wanted to talk to people whose relatives had fallen ill with the virus, looking online for reports of symptoms like fever and cough, basically anything associated with the kind of virus. He stumbled upon a guy in Shanghai, a 30-year-old architect, who told him that his healthy, normal 30-year-old wife had started to feel like she had the flu a couple of weeks earlier but then suddenly began to worsen, with a fever and trouble breathing. She was sent to a contagious disease ward, and the family was told she was likely to die. Michael Barbaro wanted to understand what was behind the illness, but he realized that he did not understand much. Days passed, and according to the family, they tried to get her tested for the coronavirus, but the doctors and medical workers refused. The family pulled out their phone to show him the death certificate that said she died of severe pneumonia. Michael Barbaro learned that testing became clear at the moment that something was going on; hospitals just were not prepared enough with testing kits and were running tests on many people, but they left just counting people anymore, even those diagnosed with the illness, and maybe even included in the official count. One thing that really stuck with him from the interview at the hospital was when he was told that bodies were burned immediately. Michael Barbaro wondered what that meant, as burning bodies began to suggest that hospital workers were starting to think the illness was contagious. They wanted the bodies burned immediately, which began to suggest that perhaps they thought it posed a threat to people. He got to thinking whether people like him went online to search social media to quickly find others reporting similar experiences. People were saying they went to hospitals and brought sick relatives, only to be turned away. He began to add things up, and it seemed like the numbers were not right. Michael Barbaro pointed out that skepticism was growing and sounding pretty warranted. Next, he headed back to his hotel to start trying to make sense of it all. Sitting in his room, he began to see reports emerging on social media. For the first time since the mysterious pneumonia-like illness broke out, Chinese health authorities admitted that the disease was contagious. One top health expert acknowledged that the virus was now spreading from person to person. An archived recording features a year-old guy who had dug into retirement and was essentially a renowned expert from the SARS crisis, suddenly telling people on social media that the crisis was much worse than previously known. Michael Barbaro notes that the doctor was saying that even in one case, a patient was able to infect medical workers. He began to see panic spreading across social media, as archived recordings warned that coronavirus could be transmitted through coughing and fever. The archived recordings indicated that the spread of the virus was accelerating, and the world began to wake up to the situation. Meanwhile, new cases were confirmed outside of China, with Thailand reporting the first case of the Wuhan coronavirus found outside of China. Archived recordings indicated that Thailand, Singapore, and possibly Scotland were bracing at airports in the United States, concerned about the growing numbers. Every day, it seemed like the numbers were just spiraling, with the death toll climbing overnight. The archived recordings indicated that the death toll from the deadly viral outbreak of the new coronavirus had surpassed previous counts. Just as the Chinese people were worried, everyone was worried and afraid of dying, hearing people wondering whether the virus would ever be contained. Michael Barbaro reflected on how he felt in that moment, interacting with people taking care of the sick and infected with the illness. He felt anxious, beginning to think that it was much worse than he had thought. He felt a sense that it was easy to settle into situations like this, with masks and washing hands all the time, but he thought about every button he touched and every surface he came into contact with, and every cough he saw around him. He felt like the virus was everywhere, and he needed to be careful. Michael Barbaro finished his reporting and grabbed a flight back to Beijing, and just one day later, during the massive New Year holiday when hundreds of millions in the country celebrate with their families, he heard that the entire city of Wuhan, with a population of millions, was placed on lockdown. The Chinese government had placed the entire city on lockdown, which was unprecedented. Michael Barbaro was shocked as trains, flights, and buses were canceled, and even public transport within Wuhan came to a ground halt. He noted that the city was basically told that everybody else remains going anywhere, as the city was closed down in a way that China had never done before, even with major modern cities. Archived recordings indicated that across China, the lockdown was expanding to contain the epidemic, and it quickly became clear that the government was facing a problem that was not just local. Travel bans were affecting dozens of cities and millions of people, forcing them to stay home. This was the biggest lockdown ever seen, and experts were saying it was the biggest experiment in public health ever seen. Archived recordings indicated that despite the efforts of the authorities, the virus could not be stopped, and much depended on whether the measures set in place by the Chinese government would prove effective. Michael Barbaro noted that it was hard to imagine how a country could mount such a response, as it seemed like an authoritarian system was in full force. People had no choice but to comply, and many were stuck trying to get health care they needed, with doctors complaining about a lack of medical supplies and critical items like masks. He got the sense that people were kind of stuck in a bargain made by living in the system, with no choice but to follow orders. Michael Barbaro reflected on how everything he learned about the Chinese authoritarian government seemed to control every aspect of their lives. He noted that the government was able to essentially drop a wall around Wuhan, knowing they could identify and control the outbreak. He thought about how the government had known how to pull off massive displays of citizen mobilization and technological control, but on the flip side, the authoritarian culture had set the stage for the crisis. He noted that for decades, China had built a ruthless system where the official Communist Party was expected to be almost perfect, and when anything went wrong, no one would take responsibility. This created an incentive system for local officials to fear saying anything bad, as they worried they would lose power. In situations like this, when a medical crisis gets really big, local officials try to contain it and keep Beijing from knowing, and those kinds of dynamics played a huge role in the scale of the SARS outbreak. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and while inflation can rise and fall based on developments and economic conditions, limited oil production and supply chain problems can exacerbate it. Inflation can be detrimental, depending on the circumstances; fast price increases can spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poorer households spend a larger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation can also affect the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. Brian, the deputy general counsel nominated to be the next general counsel, told staff members at the Senate Finance Committee confirmation hearing last week that the change could be made without a new Justice Department memorandum declaring it legal. Inflation FAQs indicate that inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow, typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, transportation, and toys. Causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, and inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation can be bad, depending on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks, while financial assets have historically fared badly during inflation booms; tangible assets like houses have held their value better. At a prior hearing, Ashley, a spokeswoman for the Democrats on the committee, indicated that the Finance Committee staff office has a legal opinion that the Treasury Department cannot unilaterally index capital gains rates for inflation. The Treasury general counsel nominee believes the department has the authority to unilaterally give the top percent nearly a billion additional tax cuts, and the issue is put to the Justice Department, which has yet to respond to a request for comment. Capital gains come from the sale of an asset, like stock or a house, that has grown in value over time, and gains on assets held by a taxpayer for a year are taxed at a maximum rate of 20 percent, which is lower than the top rate for income earned from wages; currently, gains are calculated using dollar amounts adjusted for inflation, so an investor who bought a tech stock and sold it today would owe tax on the capital gain.

Inflation FAQ card: inflation is the loss of purchasing power over time, meaning a dollar today is worth less than a dollar tomorrow, typically expressed as the annual change in prices of everyday goods and services like food, furniture, apparel, and transportation. The causes of inflation result from rising consumer demand, but inflation can also rise and fall based on developments in economic conditions, limited oil production, and supply chain problems. Inflation is bad but depends on the circumstances; fast price increases spell trouble, while moderate price gains can lead to higher wages and job growth. Inflation affects the poor especially hard, as poor households spend a bigger chunk of their budgets on necessities like food, housing, and gas. Inflation also affects the stock market, as rapid inflation typically spells trouble for stocks and financial assets in general, which have historically fared badly during inflation booms, while tangible assets like houses have held their value better. President Obama announced new limits on intelligence bulk collection of phone call records, rejecting recommendations from a panel of outside advisers for changes to government surveillance of phone records. The panel's recommendation would require court permission to search collected telephone records and restrict the number of people whose records are examined. Obama's decision accepts the recommendations, and documents released in June reveal that the NSA has been systematically collecting logs of every phone call for five years, with agency analysts examining call records of people three links removed from a number to decide ties to terrorism. Obama says he wants to find a way for the government to collect records in bulk rather than keep them in private hands. In the meantime, analysts are now able to examine records of people two degrees away from a suspect's number, and the NSA must obtain a court order ahead of time if a judge agrees that the standard of suspicion is met. The panel's recommendation to keep bulk call records in private hands rather than with the government is embraced by Obama's decision, which leaves the data in the hands of the government. Now there are two options: one requires telecommunications providers to retain calling records for a certain time to store data in a way that the government can quickly access and cross-reference records to create private records. Obama says the difficulties of these options directed the administration to study alternatives and work with Congress to find a solution. Obama rejected the idea of the program entirely, with lawmakers and civil rights advocates saying they want to retain capabilities to reduce the possibility of abuses. The panel's recommendation to cut the number of years records are retained from two to five is addressed in Obama's decision. Aides said Obama would like the NSA to stop holding data, which he deemed makes little sense, and ordered the agency to purge data quickly, leaving open the question of how long telecommunications providers are required to retain records of emails and phone calls. The panel's recommendation requires a court order to search databases containing Americans' emails and phone calls intercepted without a warrant while targeting foreigners abroad. Obama's decision includes studying additional checks, specifically mentioning court permission, and he asked the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence to come up with ideas for additional restrictions on the ability to retain, search, and use communications of Americans collected without a warrant through national security letters. The panel's recommendation requires a judge to sign national security letters, while Obama's decision reduces the secrecy of these letters by requiring court permission. National security letters and subpoenas are used by the FBI to compel businesses to turn over a range of records about customers, such as financial transactions and data communications. The FBI uses this device tens of thousands of times a year, objecting to losing power unless court approval is obtained. Obama rejected the recommendation to impose a court approval requirement, ending open-ended secrecy by stating that orders expire after a fixed period. In cases where providers are allowed to say publicly about the scope and scale of the orders they receive, the panel's recommendation suggests that the president create a process requiring the monitoring of foreign leaders unless there is a compelling national security purpose for disclosures. The NSA's surveillance of foreign leaders, including the cellphone of Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany, led to a diplomatic crisis for the Obama administration in October. Obama said there would generally be a ban on this practice, and a senior administration official stated that the list included leaders of foreign countries without addressing whether the administration would spy on top officials of those countries. The panel's recommendation to extend privacy protections for information collected from foreigners to now include citizens is part of Obama's decision, directing officials to develop new safeguards. Recent disclosures revealed that the NSA collects vast amounts of information from overseas telecommunications networks in bulk, including the contents of communications. Obama stated that new safeguards would limit the government's ability to hold personal information about foreigners and restrict its use, acknowledging a unique responsibility to ensure that foreigners overseas enjoy protections similar to those of citizens. He emphasized that the spy agencies around the world operate beyond the court structure. The panel's recommendation to create a public advocate to argue for privacy concerns in secret proceedings is included in Obama's decision, which creates a panel of advocates to represent significant privacy concerns in important cases. A senior official stated that these advocates would be called upon in cases presenting novel and important privacy law issues. The panel's recommendation to change the way judges are selected for the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court is addressed in Obama's decision, as currently, Chief Justice John Roberts appoints judges who serve as extra duty in the secret court, with the process overwhelmingly favoring Republican-appointed judges. Critics have called this court biased, and administration officials said Obama would accept changes made by Congress regarding cybersecurity. The panel's recommendation to rarely use flaws in software as a key technique for cyber surveillance warfare is addressed in Obama's decision. A speech from the White House states that recommendations for reviewing the NSA were made in July, following a report from the New York Times that the NSA was collecting previously unknown flaws in common computer programs during mounting cyberattacks. The White House indicates that the recommendation is now under review by the Security Council to adjust existing practices. The panel's recommendation to undermine or weaken generally available commercial standards is addressed in Obama's decision, with documents released in September revealing that the agency was working to weaken standards to easily crack secure systems. The White House states that the cybersecurity and science and technology offices are reviewing these issues to support the aim of protecting commercial standards. The panel's recommendation to split Cyber Command from the NSA is mentioned in Obama's decision, which has already been rejected by Defense Secretary Robert Gates, who combined the two positions, making the head of the NSA responsible for gathering intelligence for Cyber Command. Obama has already rejected the recommendation to split the command between the NSA and Cyber Command.

Though the process of counting deaths is a decades-old fact, experts say the toll of nearly COVID deaths is likely inflated. Experts say on Sunday, Governor Andrew Cuomo became the latest string of elected officials, including President Trump, to question the death toll from coronavirus, calling into question the process used to determine the cause of death. The governor also questioned the use of deaths in public, noting that New York continues to keep total death counts even though many states and New York City post publicly. Public health experts say the method used to count deaths from diseases like COVID is decades old, and the amount of uncertainty is simply part of a politically charged process. People looking to question the data, said Robert Anderson, who runs the mortality statistics branch at the Centers for Disease Control and the National Center for Health Statistics, rely on two systems in partnership with the CDC. One system, called disease surveillance, involves public health staff members and healthcare workers tracking outcomes for people with COVID infections, producing quick public numbers, while the other system involves doctors submitting death certificates to vital records offices, which work with the CDC to tally COVID deaths and create the official death toll. Washington was the first state to announce COVID deaths, and the two systems help better understand the COVID toll. Lab-confirmed deaths and COVID deaths in Washington state are based on disease surveillance, with causes related to deaths being tracked. Vital records also confirm deaths, and probable deaths are based on vital records as well. Washington uses the disease surveillance system to track deaths among people who tested positive for coronavirus, and state officials also compare death certificates with disease surveillance data to identify COVID deaths unrelated to causes like gunshot wounds. Washington removed deaths from states' staff members' data systems to compare death certificates with the disease surveillance process, and it was also found that deaths involving COVID included another cause of death, like a stroke. Many death certificates show COVID as the cause of death matching positive coronavirus cases found in disease surveillance, and a person who dies from COVID without a lab test is considered a probable death, as the CDC said. Probable deaths are a standard part of the counting process. President and conservative news media have accused states of inflating counts, but public health experts said the likely limited awareness of testing in the initial months of the pandemic means an unknown number of early COVID deaths were never counted. Washington identified additional death certificates early in the year with causes of death aligning with COVID symptoms like pneumonia, and state health officials believe a small portion of deaths are due to COVID infections. The number of dead in the United States is approaching figures compiled by the New York Times, and state health officials are grappling with the demand for real-time information, taking different approaches to share information with the public. Half of states are now reporting probable deaths to the CDC on public health department websites, although sometimes states report deaths as lab-confirmed. Washington is one of several states tracking probable deaths internally, though it announced on Wednesday that it would include these deaths in the state total next month. The CDC asked states to start reporting probable deaths in April based on guidance from the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists, citing a lack of COVID surveillance among states that counted only lab-confirmed deaths. Janet Hamilton, executive director of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists, said that the number of individuals who died is agreed upon. States are facing the challenge of providing immediate and accurate information critical for informing policy decisions and restrictions on businesses and social activities. This expectation is complicated by limited testing and the lengthy process of investigating deaths, which can take weeks or even months. Many states' data tracking systems date back years, and as the disease moves at the speed and intensity of COVID, there is an absolute need for data, Hamilton said. States still rely on mail and phone for disease surveillance, while a handful of states use paper systems for death certificates. The two systems help states count deaths with certainty, and typically, public health staff talk about certain deaths during the pandemic to reconcile differences. A growing number of states regularly report probable deaths alongside lab-confirmed deaths, while states track probable deaths internally yet do not include them in public reports. States publicly report confirmed and probable deaths separately, and early to mid-June saw probable deaths make up a small share of total deaths reported by states, commonly ranging from one to five percent, with some states reporting as much as one-quarter of total deaths. Many probable deaths involve outbreaks in nursing homes where residents get tested, and even states that chose to report probable deaths need time to process mortality data. Deaths counted from death certificate data are sent to the National Center for Health Statistics, which uses COVID death counts along with total deaths and causes to determine the number of excess deaths during the pandemic, offering a better picture of the COVID death toll. Experts expect the exact tally of deaths from the disease to be widely accepted, similar to flu death certificates, and the CDC reports annual flu deaths in a broad range. The federal government helps the country better understand the COVID death toll, and right now, said Charles, former director of the National Center for Health Statistics, frontline workers like medical personnel need upgraded reporting systems for health records, vital records, and disease tracking, with federal guidance connected to the possible expense.

The vaccine developed by the University of Oxford and AstraZeneca has the potential to slow the transmission of the virus, according to a new paper from researchers at the University of Oxford. The latest report provides evidence suggesting the coronavirus vaccine is able to reduce the transmission of the virus, though scientists emphasized that the data is preliminary and the degree of protection is unknown. Researchers measured the impact on transmission among participants every week, seeking to detect signs of the virus, and found a percent reduction in positive cases among vaccinated individuals. The paper, which is peer-reviewed, looked at data from clinical trials in Britain, Brazil, and South Africa, with results first reported late last year. Matt, the British health secretary, hailed the results on Wednesday, stating, "We now know the Oxford vaccine also reduces transmission, which helps get us out of the pandemic," in an interview on Wednesday morning with the BBC. He added that the results should give everyone confidence that it works to keep safe and prevent passing the virus. Scientists, looking at the limited information released, cautioned that analysis of the data is needed to draw broad conclusions, but firmly stated it is extremely welcome news. "We need the data confirmed; it is important to still continue to follow social distancing guidance," said Doug Brown, chief executive of the British Society. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers also found that a single dose of the vaccine is percent effective in preventing COVID, with data measured three months after the first shot was given, including the initial three-week period needed for protection to take effect. These encouraging results lend support to the strategy deployed in Britain and other countries to prioritize providing as many first doses of vaccines as possible, setting aside concerns about people getting their second doses later than initially planned. The latest data bears on the debate regarding the spacing of doses for the two vaccines authorized in the United States, Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, since data from candidate vaccines prompted scientists to call for the United States to follow the lead of Britain, which opted to delay second doses for weeks. Federal officials resisted, saying the move was not supported by data from clinical trials of the two vaccines currently available across the nation. The results amplify pressure on health officials to delay second doses of the vaccine, though it has not yet been authorized in the country. The vaccine appeared effective with two shots, longer than the originally intended four-week gap. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers found that among clinical trial participants who received two standard-strength doses at least three months apart, the vaccine was percent effective compared to percent effective for doses given less than six weeks apart. The vaccination strategy of spacing doses by three months was necessary due to limited vaccine supplies in the short term, and researchers wrote in a newly released paper that builds on data issued late last year, finding the vaccine percent effective when given in two standard-strength doses. Initial findings showed efficacy much higher percent for the first dose of the vaccine given at half strength. Oxford AstraZeneca researchers initially attributed the different levels of effectiveness to the lower strength of the initial dose but gradually reached a different conclusion, with the amount of time between doses likely being the explanation. The United States Food and Drug Administration is waiting for data from a clinical trial that enrolled participants mostly from America, with results from the study expected later this month. The study is expected to arm AstraZeneca with enough safety data to allow it to seek authorization to provide the vaccine for emergency use in the United States, which agreed to buy million doses of the vaccine, although neither company nor the federal government has specified the quantities of doses available once the vaccine is approved.

Despite high tech tools, authorities mainly rely on flood workers to keep hundreds of millions of people coming into contact with outsiders to tame the coronavirus. Mao-style social control blankets China, as in Shanghai, where flooded cities and villages see neighborhood uniformed volunteers and Communist Party representatives carry out one of the biggest social control campaigns in history. The goal is to keep hundreds of millions of people away from everyone, as the nation battles the coronavirus outbreak through grassroots mobilization reminiscent of Mao-style mass movements seen in China decades ago. Essentially, this is a front line epidemic prevention version of a neighborhood watch. Housing in cities is issued paper hall passes to regulate how often residents leave their homes, and apartment buildings turn away tenants coming into town. Train stations block people entering cities to prove they live or work in countryside villages, while vehicles and tents serve as improvised barriers. Despite an arsenal of high tech surveillance tools, controls are mainly enforced by hundreds of thousands of workers and volunteers who check temperatures, log movements, and oversee quarantines, which is important to keep away outsiders who might carry the virus.

Linking immigration to crime exists as a myth; Americans see nowhere else but in Trump’s first year, as immigration policy relied on claims that immigrants bring crime to America. The president's latest target is sanctuary cities, as he stated that sanctuary cities release illegal immigrants, drug dealers, and gang members back into communities. He said last week that it is just terrible, and according to polls, almost half of Americans agreed that immigrants make crime worse. While it is true that immigration drives crime, many studies have shown that immigrant populations in the United States have been growing fast for decades, while crime has moved in the opposite direction. The national rate of violent crime today reflects large-scale collaboration from four universities led by Robert, a sociologist at the State University of New York at Buffalo. Researchers compared immigration rates and crime rates in metropolitan areas over the last several decades, selecting areas that included huge urban hubs like New York and smaller manufacturing centers of less size, like Indiana, across the country. According to the data from the study, the large majority of areas with many immigrants today have fewer violent crimes. The Marshall Project extended data showing that crime fell or often rose even as immigrant populations grew almost across the board in metro areas. Almost 50 percent of those studied showed that when the immigrant population increased, crime stayed stable or fell in a number of areas. In areas where crime increased, the immigration levels were much lower, with slightly over a quarter of total places showing the largest increases in immigrants alongside lower levels of crime. Yet, the argument that immigrants bring crime to America is driven by many policies enacted and proposed by the administration, including far-reaching restrictions on entry, travel visas, heightened border enforcement, and plans for a wall along the border with Mexico. Last month, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit against California in response to restrictions on local police assisting Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers with undocumented immigrants charged with crimes. On Tuesday, Orange County signed support for the suit, noting that the immigrant population in the county doubled since overall violent crime decreased by 20 percent. A similar pattern emerged in two places: Trump recently mentioned local leaders in Oakland, California, and Lawrence, Massachusetts, describing these cities as grounds for drugs and crime brought by immigrants. In Oakland, like Orange County, increasing immigration coincided with falling crime. In Lawrence, though murder and robbery rates grew, overall violent crime rates still fell by 20 percent. General data suggests either immigration has an effect on reducing average crime or there is simply a relationship between the two areas. The study grew instances of coincidence and cause-effect, showing a consistent pattern over a decade where immigrant populations and crime failed to grow together. In the majority of areas, the number of immigrants increased by at least 20 percent, with the greatest increases occurring early on while violent crime rates in those areas ranged from a 30 percent decline to a 10 percent rise. Often, in places with a sharp rise in immigrant population, increases in crime rates frequently followed modest growth in immigration, with the average immigrant population growing by 20 percent while the average crime fell by 10 percent during that period. The FBI changed how rape was defined in crime figures, and the analysis focused on components of the violent crime rate, such as assaults and murders, but still fails to reveal the relationship between immigration rates and the immigrant population. Assault rates ranged from a 30 percent decline to a 20 percent rise, robbery rates declined in a range of 10 percent to 30 percent, and murder rates declined in a range of 20 percent to 10 percent. One comprehensive study of local immigrant crime relationships over decades in metropolitan areas shows that the data from places with widely varying social, cultural, and economic backgrounds reflects a broad range of types of violent crime. Areas chosen reflect a range of immigrant composition, with one area having every second person born outside the United States. In areas with newly formed immigrant communities and immigrant pockets that have gone back generations, controlling for population characteristics, unemployment rates, and conditions, researchers still found that average immigration increases American crime. The foreign-born data collected by the Census likely numbers undocumented immigrants, many of whom wish to avoid the risk of identifying themselves; however, they are at least partly represented in the overall foreign-born population counts. The study shows that immigration does not increase crime, and a broad survey released in January examined years of research on the immigrant crime connection, concluding that the overwhelming majority of studies found either a beneficial relationship between the two or that immigrant communities bring economic and cultural benefits to neighborhoods. Central bankers voted unanimously to make this unusually large interest rate move, and the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee signaled in a post-meeting statement that ongoing increases in the target range for the policy rate will affect borrowing costs, now set in a range of percent. The Fed began raising interest rates from near zero in March, and policymakers have picked up the pace since, making a quarter point move to start and then raising by half a point and three quarters of a point in June, the largest single step since the Fed officials made the second increase on Wednesday, trying urgently to wrestle rapid inflation back under control. Takeaways from the decision include Fed Chair Jerome Powell's post-meeting news conference, where he indicated that another big rate move is coming in September, and Powell made it clear that a third large three-quarter point rate increase is possible at the next meeting. It has been a long time since officials have been watching new pieces of data to make decisions, and Powell thinks a recession is highlighted by evidence of the economy slowing, though it is not yet clear how much. Powell also pointed to the strength of the labor market as a reason to think the economy is currently not in a downturn, but he cautioned that fresh data on economic growth set to be released Thursday could indicate that a downturn is inevitable. Powell said he thinks a slowdown is assured, though he highlighted that it is difficult to lower inflation without one, and he noted that the path toward avoiding a downturn requires growth to slow. Powell said that a slowing economy is a good perspective, and he emphasized that cooling economic activity enough to lower inflation will probably involve weakening the labor market a little bit, with some pain necessary now to put the economy on a sustainable path. He wants bigger needs, and Powell said that thinking about medium to long-term stability makes the whole economy better. These comments are precisely what stock investors wanted to hear, as investors are worried about the Fed tipping the American economy into recession. On Wall Street, Wednesday's signals from the Fed indicated a slow pace of interest rate increases in the future, and Powell is aware of early signs of a slowdown in the economy. The stock index ended the day up percent, posting its best day since April, but markets can quickly change their tune, especially with new data on growth coming Thursday. In the last two times the Fed raised rates, the market rallied on the day of the announcement but fell sharply the following day.

The article in the journal Science reported that a type of machine learning, which focuses on human capabilities in a narrow range of vision-related tasks, is advancing artificial intelligence to rival human abilities. This new approach, known as program learning, differs from current machine learning technologies, which are known as deep networks. These networks are trained to recognize human speech, detect objects in images, and identify kinds of behavior by being exposed to large sets of examples. Although these networks model behavior biologically, they do not learn in the same way humans do, acquiring new knowledge quickly. In contrast, the new software program described in the Science article is able to learn to recognize characters from even a single example. Researchers compared the capabilities of this approach to programming models using five separate learning tasks involving a set of characters from a research data set, which includes character sets from various languages and images of pen strokes needed to create characters. "Captured progress in machine learning is amazing," said Joshua, a professor of cognitive science at MIT and one of the authors of the Science paper. "Look at how children learn with little data; it comes from prior knowledge that is built."
